4.18 Conclusion
During the year 2023-24, all the Controlling Officers reconciled the Government receipts 
and expenditure with the figures in the books of the Sr. DAG (A&E).
Audit observed that ₹7.75 crore was required to be paid as interest on the balance of 
₹290.24 crore lying under interest bearing deposits/Reserve Funds. Non-payment/short 
payment of the interest amounting to ₹7.75 crore has resulted in understatement of 
Revenue Expenditure and Fiscal Deficit by ₹7.75 crore.
Revenue Receipts of ₹359.02 crore earned from sale proceeds of electricity sold outside 
the State and royalty receipts from the HEPs located in the State, were not deposited in 
the Consolidated Fund of State by PDS. This led to understatement of Revenue Receipts 
by ₹359.02 crore. Further, an expenditure of ₹ 359.02 crore had been incurred without 

State Finances Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2024
112
routing it through Government Accounts resulting in understatement of Government 
expenditure by ₹359.02 crore. 
Classification of large amounts under the omnibus Minor Head 800 affects transparency 
in financial reporting and distorts proper analysis of allocative priorities and quality of 
expenditure.
It has been found that 980 UCs amounting to ₹122.18 crore was due for submission on 
or before 31 March 2024.
It was seen that during 2023-24, ₹24.83 crore (36 per cent) was drawn through 245 AC 
Bills in March 2024.
Audit observed that non-furnishing of detailed information about financial assistance 
given to various institutions and non-submission of accounts by 135 accounts 
Autonomous Bodies/ Authorities as per timelines led to non-compliance with Financial 
Rules. There were also delays in placement of SARs to Legislature. 
There were cases of misappropriation involving Government money in respect of seven 
Departments with the money value of ₹ 2.86 crore at the end of 2023-24 where final 
action was pending.
4.19  Recommendations
	 Departments should adhere to the Government Accounting Rules and all the 
financial transactions should be routed through Government Accounts to reflect 
actual financial position of the State.
	 Finance Department may draw up action plan for monitoring and ensuring 
submission of all pending UCs especially keeping in view that UCs from  
2002-03 onwards are still due for submission.  Release of subsequent grants should 
be linked with submission of outstanding UCs.
	 Finance Department may make special efforts to settle old outstanding AC bills 
specially keeping in view that submission of DC bills from 2001-02 onwards are still 
pending for submission.  At the same time, the DDOs should be asked to ensure that 
the DC bills are submitted within prescribed time, in order to avoid accumulation 
of unadjusted AC bills. Advances should be monitored closely for effective control 
and old outstanding AC bills should be adjusted by making special efforts in a time 
bound manner.
	 Timely reconciliation may be done with figures of the P AO and office of the Sr. 
DAG (A&E) to avoid discrepancies in Accounts. Special efforts need to be taken 
for reconciliation of balances in State Bank of Sikkim and P AO figures.
	 To make accounts transparent, the Government should operate appropriate Minor 
Heads instead of booking under Minor Head 800.

Chapter IV: Quality of Accounts and Financial Reporting Practices 
113
	 Finance Department should consider evolving a system to expedite the process 
of compilation and submission of annual accounts by autonomous bodies for 
reporting of their financial position.
	 The Government should prepare a time bound framework for taking prompt action 
in cases of misappropriation, loss, theft, etc., and for strengthening the internal 
control system in Departments to prevent recurrence of such cases.

Appendix 1.1
Part C: Structure of Government Accounts
(Reference: Paragraph 1.3)
The accounts of the State Government are kept in three parts viz., Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund 
and Public Account.
Part I: Consolidated Fund: All revenues received by the State Government, all loans raised by issue of 
treasury bills, internal loans and all moneys received by the Government in repayment of loans shall form 
one Consolidated Fund entitled the Consolidated Fund of the State established under Article 266 (1) of 
the Constitution of India.
Part II: Contingency Fund:  Contingency Fund of the State established under Article 267(2) of the 
Constitution is in the nature of an imprest placed at the disposal of the Governor to enable him to make 
advances to meet urgent unforeseen expenditure, pending authorisation by the Legislature. Approval of 
the Legislature for such expenditure and for withdrawal of an equivalent amount from the Consolidated 
Fund is subsequently obtained, whereupon the advances from the Contingency Fund are recouped to the 
fund.
Part III: Public Account:  Receipts and disbursements in respect of certain transactions such as small 
savings, provident funds, reserve funds, deposits, suspense, remittances etc., which do not form part of 
the Consolidated Fund, are kept in the Public Account set up under Article 266(2) of the Constitution and 
are not subject to vote by the State Legislature.

The compound annual growth rate is calculated by taking the nth root of 
the total percentage growth rate, where n is the number of years in the 
period being considered.
CAGR = [Ending Value/Beginning Value] (1/no. of years) -1
GSDP
GSDP is defined as the total income of the State or the market value 
of goods and services produced using labour and all other factors of 
production at current prices.
Buoyancy Ratio
Buoyancy ratio indicates the elasticity or degree of responsiveness of a 
fiscal variable with respect to a given change in the base variable. For 
instance, revenue buoyancy at 0.7 implies that revenue receipts tend to 
increase by 0.7 percentage points, if the GSDP increases by one per cent.

Terms Basis of Calculation
Core Public and Merit 
Goods
Core public goods are those which all citizens enjoy in common in 
the sense that each individual’s consumption of such goods lead to no 
subtractions from any other individual’s consumption of that goods, 
e.g. enforcement of law and order, security and protection of our rights; 
pollution free air, other environmental good, road infrastructure etc. 
Merit goods are commodities that the public sector provides free or at 
subsidised rates because an individual or society should have them on the 
basis of some concept of need, rather than ability and willingness to pay 
the Government and therefore wishes to encourage their consumption. 
Examples of such goods include the provision of free or subsidised food 
for the poor to support nutrition, delivery of health services to improve 
quality of life and reduce morbidity, providing basic education to all, 
drinking water and sanitation, etc.
“The analysis of expenditure data is disaggregated into developmental 
and non-developmental expenditure. All expenditure relating to Revenue 
Account, Capital Outlay and Loans and Advances is categorised into 
social services, economic services and general services. Broadly, the 
social and economic services constitute developmental expenditure, 
while expenditure on general services is treated as non-developmental 
expenditure
Debt Sustainability
The Debt sustainability is defined as the ability of the State to maintain 
a constant debt- GSDP ratio over a period of time and also embodies 
the concern about the ability to service its debt. Sustainability of debt 
therefore also refers to sufficiency of liquid assets to meet current or 
committed obligations and the capacity to keep balance between costs of 
additional borrowings with returns from such borrowings. It means that 
rise in fiscal deficit should match with the increase in capacity to service 
the debt.
Non-debt Receipts
Adequacy of incremental non-debt receipts of the State to cover the 
incremental interest liabilities and incremental primary expenditure. The 
debt sustainability could be significantly facilitated if the incremental 
non-debt receipts could meet the incremental interest burden and the 
incremental primary expenditure.
Net Availability of 
Borrowed Funds
Defined as the ratio of the debt redemption (principal+ interest payments) 
to total debt receipts indicates the extent to which the debt receipts are 
used in debt redemption and gives the net availability of borrowed funds.

OVERVIEW

OVERVIEW
This Audit Report consists of eight chapters, which deal with Social, Economic, 
Economic (Public Sector Undertakings), Revenue, General Sectors and Local Bodies. 
Chapter VIII deals with Follow up action on earlier Audit, reports and response of 
departments to recommendations of the Public Account Committee. 
This Report also includes three Performance Audits viz. Performance Audit on Building 
and Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess, Implementation of Pradhan Mantri 
Gram Sadak Yojana and Solid Waste Management in Urban Local Bodies, four Subject 
Specific Compliance Audits (SSCA) on Public Health Infrastructure and Management 
of Health Services, Department oversight on GST payment and return filing, Swadesh 
Darshan Scheme and Efficacy of implementation of 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 
in Sikkim. The Report was forwarded to the Secretary of the Departments concerned 
with a request to furnish replies to the observations. Replies received have been suitably 
incorporated in the Report. 
SOCIAL SECTOR 
The Chapter on Social Sector consists of one Performance Audit and one Subject 
Specific Compliance Audit. 
PERFORMANCE AUDIT 
BUILDING AND OTHER CONSTRUCTION WORKERS WELFARE CESS
Government of India (GoI) enacted the Building and Other Construction Workers’ 
(Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996  (BOCW Act) and 
Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1996 (Cess Act). The Acts 
aimed to provide safety, health and welfare measures for the benefit of building and 
other construction (BOC) workers through levy of cess.
Government of Sikkim (GoS) notified (August 2010) the Sikkim Building and Other 
Construction Workers (SBOCW) Rules, 2010. The collection of BOCW cess was fixed 
at the rate of one per cent on the cost of construction incurred by the employers.
Audit observations
The Board did not prepare annual budget estimates upto 2021-22.  In the absence of an 
annual budget, the Board could not effectively plan and manage its financial resources to 
support the implementation of various programmes and projects to promote the welfare 
of BOC workers.
(Paragraph 2.3.8.2)
Audit observed that during 2017-18 to 2021-22, the Board had invested ₹ 73.44 crore in 
non-nationalised banks (IDBI Bank, Yes Bank, Axis Bank, ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, 
etc.), which was in contravention to the directions of the Supreme Court and the SBOCW 
rules, 2010.
(Paragraph 2.3.8.3)

Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2023
vi
The Board incurred administrative expenditure ranging from 3.48 per cent and 65.93 per 
cent during the period from 2017-18 to 2021-22, with five per cent being the maximum 
limit.
(Paragraph 2.3.8.4)
The Board had not maintained details of workers viz., name, contact numbers, Certificate 
for age proof and address proof, Bank details, family details for nomination, etc. which 
were required to be submitted by the employer. The Board also failed to produce to 
Audit year-wise list of registered workers for the period 2017-22. 
(Paragraph 2.3.10.1)
The establishment register maintained by the Board only included manual entries of 
those establishments or employers who had applied for registration, leaving many 
unregistered entities outside its purview. The Board did not conduct any inspection 
to assess eligibility for registration of establishments carrying out works where 10 or 
more workers were employed by the employer, towards ensuring their registration. 
Due to non-identification of all unregistered establishments and non-maintenance of 
a comprehensive database for capturing details of all establishments or employers, the 
Board not only could not ensure implementation of welfare benefits for all BOC workers 
but also could not assess and collect the actual cess receivable from these establishments.
(Paragraph 2.3.10.2)
The system of providing Universal Access Number/Unique Identification Number  
to construction workers was not introduced by the Board during the period of audit  
(2017-22).
(Paragraph 2.3.10.5)
Audit scrutiny showed that none of the employers carrying out building or other 
construction works under the Board’s record had furnished returns showing the details 
of workers entitled to be registered as well as those who left the service during the 
preceding month and particulars of the establishment, during 2017-22.

SUBJECT SPECIFIC COMPLIANCE AUDIT 
PUBLIC HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE AND MANAGEMENT OF HEALTH 
SERVICES 
The public healthcare delivery system in India is organised at three levels – primary, 
secondary, and tertiary. The vast network of Primary Health Sub-Centres (SCs), Primary 
Health Centres (PHCs), Urban Primary Health Centres (UPHCs) and Community Health 
Centres (CHCs) form the primary tier of public healthcare delivery system for rural and 
urban population. District Hospitals (DHs) provide secondary-level healthcare services 
for rural and urban populations. These hospitals handle the treatment and management of 
diseases or medical conditions that require specialised care. Tertiary healthcare involves 
providing advanced and super-specialty services to be provided by medical institutions 
in urban areas, which are well equipped with sophisticated diagnostic and investigative 
facilities. 
Audit Observations
The State Government had not formulated any policy or strategy in line with the National 
Health Policy 2017 (NHP 17) till March 2023, to determine the size of budget to be 
allocated to the Health Sector, either as percentage of the overall State budget or the 

Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2023
viii
GSDP. The State did not achieve the NHP stipulated eight per cent budgetary allocation 
for health sector in any of the five years during the period 2017-22.
(Paragraph 2.4.22.1)
The budget allocation/ expenditure on maintenance of hospitals, health centres and other 
buildings was on a decreasing trend since 2019-20 despite addition of five new health-
care facilities and increase in bed capacity by 770 units over the period 2017-22.
 (Paragraph 2.4.22.4)
The newly constructed PHC at Chipsu was lying unused, rendering an expenditure of ₹ 
6.23 crore idle. 
(Paragraph 2.4.22.5)
DHs ( Singtam, Geyzing) had no General Surgery Department to undertake major 
surgeries, etc. The Rhenock CHC also did not have blood storage facility as required 
under the IPHS. Further, there was no surgeon posted in the CHC therefore OT facility 
could not provide required services and was used to provide only basic first aid and 
minor surgical procedures like suturing, dressing of minor injuries, wounds, abscess,

In the PHCs, one to two additional medical officers beyond the IPHS norms were

not have any specialist. The CHC also did not have medical Superintendent, Public 
Health Specialist and Public Health Nurse, as required under the IPHS. Shortages and

IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PRADHAN MANTRI GRAM SADAK YOJANA 
(PMGSY)
Government of India (GoI) launched the centrally sponsored ‘ Pradhan Mantri Gram 
Sadak Yojana’ (PMGSY) in December 2000 for providing all-weather road connectivity 
to all eligible unconnected habitations in rural areas with a population of 500 persons 
and above in plain areas and 250 persons in hilly areas. Besides, upgradation of existing 
rural roads was also to be carried out under PMGSY . Further, as the Programme 
unfolded, a dire need to consolidate the entire rural road network by upgradation of 
selected Through Routes and some Major Rural Links (MRLs) was felt and accordingly 
a new intervention was evolved in May 2013 namely PMGSY-II. PMGSY–II envisages

consolidation of the existing Rural Road Network by covering upgradation of selected 
rural roads based on their economic potential and their role in facilitating the growth of 
rural market centres and rural hubs.

₹ 16.44 crore, and Maintenance ₹ 28.46 crore) was incurred during 2017-23 on 
construction, upgradation, and maintenance of rural roads under PMGSY . During the period 
covered, 433 projects (Roads-178, Bridges-97, upgradation-34 and Maintenance-124) 
were either ongoing or completed or under maintenance in the said period.

SUBJECT SPECIFIC COMPLIANCE AUDIT 
“OVERSIGHT ON GST PAYMENTS AND RETURNS FILING” FOR THE 
YEAR 2017-18
Subject Specific Compliance Audit on transitional credits under GST in Sikkim was 
taken up with a view to seeking an assurance on whether the mechanism envisaged by 
the Department for selection and verification of transitional credit claims was adequate 
and effective (System issues) and whether the transitional credits carried over by the 
individual taxpayers into GST regime were valid and admissible (Compliance issues).
Audit Observations
Audit observed that out of total 10940 taxpayers, only four taxpayers were scrutinised 
by the Commercial Taxes Division, Finance Department, Government of Sikkim and 
ASMT-10 were issued during the period from 2017-18 to 2020-21. Further, the modalities 
of scrutiny adopted by the CTD, the basis for selection of taxpayers for scrutiny, the 
checks that were done in the application itself, any data analytics methods adopted and 
reports of Directorate General of Analytics and Risk Management (DGARM) received, 
if any, and action taken thereon were called for (September 2022) in Audit, but the CTD 
had not responded till date (November 2023). Further, Audit observed that out of the 
fourteen taxpayers selected for detailed audit, three had filed GSTR-1 return(s) after a 
delay of more than six months, three had filed GSTR-3B returns after a delay of more 
than six months and two taxpayers had not filed GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C till July 2023. 
Yet no action for cancellation of their registration was seen to have been initiated by the 
CTD (November 2023).
(Paragraph 5.12.6.1)
Audit selected a sample of 93 cases (18 from Industries Sector, 46 from Service Sector 
and 29 from Trading Sector) from amongst the top deviations/inconsistencies in each of 
the 12 parameters for the year 2017-18. The audit queries were issued to the respective 
Sectors on 19 May 2022. Audit checks in these cases were limited to verifying the 
CTD’s action on the identified deviations/mismatches. Out of 93 queries issued, 
responses were received in 38 cases and no response was received (November 2023) in 
55 cases. Further, out of total 93 inconsistencies/mismatches pointed out by Audit, the 
CTD provided responses in case of 38 inconsistencies/mismatches amounting to ₹ 10.52 
crore. Out of those 38 replies, Audit noticed deviations from the provisions of the SGST 
Act in 22 cases involving amount of ₹ 3.71 crore. Out of 22 compliance deviations, the 
CTD accepted audit observations and made recoveries in four cases with tax effect of ₹ 
0.24 crore and in 18 cases, the replies were not acceptable to Audit. Out of 38 cases, in 
16 cases, the Department’s reply was acceptable to Audit, which includes 4 cases of data 
entry errors and 12 cases under other valid explanations.
(Paragraph 5.12.6.2)
Recommendations:
After evaluation of records furnished and analysis of data available in the State system, 
the following recommendations are made:

Overview
xv
	The CTD may put in place proper mechanism for scrutiny of returns to ensure 
compliance of rules pertaining to returns filing and tax payments by all taxpayers. 
The CTD may prepare a Standard Operating Procedure for manual scrutiny of 
returns in line with one prepared by CBIC, for use till automation of scrutiny is 
completed.
	CTD may establish mechanism to regularly identify late-filers and non-filers and 
take necessary steps to recover tax, interest and late fee from them.
	CTD may establish mechanism to regularly identify taxpayers who have not filed 
GST returns for more than six months and take necessary steps to recover applicable 
tax, interest and late fee from them and cancel the registrations.
	CTD may urgently pursue the 55 inconsistencies/deviations pointed out by Audit 
for which responses have not been provided and intimate the results there-of.
	The CTD may conduct similar data analysis (as conducted by Audit for Centralised/ 
limited Audit) of GST returns and other related data of all the taxpayers under State 
jurisdiction to identify inconsistencies and take necessary steps to recover dues 
from the taxpayers wherever applicable.

SUBJECT SPECIFIC COMPLIANCE AUDIT 
SWADESH DARSHAN SCHEME
Swadesh Darshan is the flagship scheme of Ministry of Tourism (MoT) of Government 
of India (GoI) for development of tourism infrastructure in the country. MoT launched 
this Central Sector Scheme in January 2015. The objective of the scheme was to develop 
tourist circuits and promote cultural and heritage value of the country. The MoT approved 
two projects Swadesh Darshan-I (SD-I) and Swadesh Darshan-II (SDII) under North-
East Circuit for the state of Sikkim. The entry point defined in SDI was at Rangpo and 
exit point was at Singtam. In respect of Swadesh Darshan -II the entry point was at 
Singtam and exit point at Melli. A Subject Specific Compliance Audit on SD, brought 
out the following significant findings:
Audit Observations
Identification of the tourist circuit and the destinations is a vital component of the 
scheme. The tourist circuits/destinations were to be identified by MoT in consultations 
with the stakeholders and States based on a pre-dominant tourism theme, considering 
certain factors. However, DPR prepared by the department did not have any reference 
to consultations. Such deficiencies in planning affected the overall execution and 
implementation of the projects resulting in instances of delay in completion of the 
projects, non-utilisation of infrastructure and improper utilisation of infrastructure 
created.
(Paragraph 6.3.8.1)

Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2023
xvi
The GoI released ₹ 187.95 crore to the State Government for SD-I & SD-II. The 
department carried out 127 works under 35 selected components, out of which 126 
works were handed over to the Assets cell of the Department by the Engineering cell 
after completion of the works for leasing out and one asset (Development of Adventure 
Tourism with International Standard Zip line from Hathipailay to Aritar Lake) was not 
handed over to asset cell. However, out of 127 assets, only 19 assets were being utilised 
for the purposes for which they were created, 77 were lying unutilised till the date of 
audit and 31 were being used for other unintended purposes. This led to infructuous 
expenditure of ₹ 17.68 crore and idling of assets valuing ₹ 18.98 crore. 
(Paragraph 6.3.9)
As per guidelines/revised guidelines, improvement/investment in assets/structures 
owned by the private entities were not admissible under the schemes. TCAD submitted 
the land availability certificate along with the DPR to MoT stating that all lands were 
free from encumbrance to accommodate all features of the project and the lands were 
in possession of the Department. However, tourist infrastructure in nine destinations 
was constructed in the land belonging to either Monastery or temple, which affected the 
State’s ownership of the project/assets as well as its access to revenue from the project.
(Paragraph 6.3.9.1)
Projects under Swadesh Darshan-I and II were sanctioned by the GoI on 30.06.2015 and 
16.09.2016 respectively. However, there was an inordinate delay in awarding tenders for 
SD-I and II. The delay in finalisation of tenders ranged from 139 days to 419 days (SD-
I) and 90 days to 243 days (SD-II) from the due date of award of tender (three months 
from the date of sanction) due to belated process for tendering, retendering due to non-
fulfillment of tendered conditions, etc.
(Paragraph 6.3.9.2)
None of the 35 components under 21 destinations (SD-I: 13 and SD-II 8) selected by 
audit were completed within the stipulated time schedule. Works were delayed ranging 
from four months to 37 months from the stipulated date of completion.
(Paragraph 6.3.9.3)
According to Paragraph 2 (20) of the Sikkim Public Works Code 2009, Contingencies 
(Works) when used in respect of the accounts of a work, indicate incidental expenses of 
a sundry nature, which cannot be classified under any Sub-head or sub-work but pertain 
to the work. However, the Department had incurred ₹ 1.85 crore on procurement of ten 
vehicles and on items which were not related to the schemes/works under SD, which 
was irregular. 
(Paragraph 6.3.10.4)
As per revised guidelines of the scheme 2017, the States UT Administration shall 
appoint a State Level Monitoring Committee for timely implementation of the project. 
The purpose of the committee is to provide feedback on the progress of implementation 
to GoI regularly. Accordingly, the Department constituted a monitoring committee 
consisting of six members headed by Chief Engineer as Chairman on 10.02.2016, 
however after a lapse of seven months of issue of sanctioned letter. However, no records 

Overview
xvii
were made available at the department to indicate that SLMC met regularly after its 
formation. In absence of monitoring mechanism, delay in completion of works ranging 
from four months to 37 months, could not be avoided. 
(Paragraph 6.3.11.1)
Recommendations:
	 Department should ensure that before selection of a project, proper survey, 
feasibility studies and consultation with shareholders are ensured. DPR should 
spell out clearly the reasons for selection of a project. No deviation from approved 
DPR shall be permitted unless absolutely necessary.
	 Department shall make every effort to ensure that the assets created under Swadesh 
Darshan I and Swadesh Darshan II are utilised for the purpose for which they 
were created.
	 Department shall ensure that a proper monitoring system may be developed to 
capture key data pertaining to tourist footfall, employment generation for effective 
implementation of the scheme.
	 The issue of construction of infrastructure at Monastery and Temple premises may 
be taken up with GoI for regularisation.

SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT (SWM)
Government of Sikkim (GoS), in the State Policy on Solid Waste Management Strategy 
notified in April 2019 has envisioned to establish a ‘Zero Waste System’ for Solid Waste 
Management in the state by the year 2030 with a mission to enable the community to 
visualise experience and own up utilisation of resources along with conservation of

Audit Observations
Even four years after the policy initiative was approved in 2019, as of June 2023, only 
two (out of seven) ULBs had decentralised solid waste processing facilities at Mangan 
Nagar Panchayat (MNP) and Gangtok Municipal Corporation (GMC).
(Paragraph 7.3.9.1)
The data on waste generated, as submitted by ULBs was based on estimation without 
assessing the quantity and composition of waste generated through sample collection.
(Paragraph 7.3.9.3)
The test checked ULBs had not carried out assessment of the financial viability of SWM 
services on a stand-alone basis to ensure their sustainability. While the user charges 

Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2023
xviii
were not realised in full by two ULBs (GyNP and MNP), the ULBs were dependent on 
government grants for SWM services to the extent of 35 to 94 per cent as only 6 to 65 
per cent of expenditure on SWM services was met from own source of revenue (user 
charges/ outsourced contract fees).

Joint physical verification showed that the source segregation of waste was not being 
carried out by majority of the households. The households bring in waste in single bin 
without segregating, dump the unsegregated waste in the garbage truck, which did not 
have separate compartment for dry and wet waste, thereby indicating lack of efforts at 
segregation.
(Paragraph 7.3.11.3)
Vehicles used for door-to-door collection of waste were uncovered (open top) and non- 
compartmentalised (no separate compartment for carrying wet and dry waste). Further, 
staff deployed for door-to-door collection were not found to be using protective gears.
(Paragraph 7.3.11.4)
The performance of the ULBs regarding processing of waste was very minimal, ranging 
between 17 and 34.51 per cent of waste generation, due to limited number of processing 
units (51.80 tpd capacity), majority (50 tpd) of which (at Martam and Gangtok) were 
non-functional from November 2021 to January 2023 and again from June 2023. A 
total of 20.2 (out of 56.55) TPD was processed during 2021-22 by four test checked 
ULBs. However, no facility to convert waste to energy by applying technology such as 
incineration, gasification, pyrolysis, or any other technology was available with ULBs. 
Waste to energy plant was not set up in any of test checked ULBs during 2018-23.
(Paragraph 7.3.11.6)
ULBs did not have sanitary landfill sites for disposal of solid waste, except for Gangtok 
town, operated by GMC. Three (out of 7) ULBs (NNP, NJNP and GyNP) used dumping 
yard at Sipchu in West Sikkim for disposal of waste. 
(Paragraph 7.3.12)
The only sanitary landfill (SLF) at Martam, initially designed for 25 years (up to 2040) 
for catering to only one ULB (Gangtok MC), was catering to four ULBs as of March 
2023. Due to excessive dumping of mixed waste, coupled with very limited processing

of waste, the shelf life  of landfill would end within two years (2025), requiring urgent

(Paragraph 7.3.12.1)
The monitoring by UDD and ULB was lax as direction of State Level Committee (SLC) 
and National Green Tribunal (NGT) was not acted upon as of June 2023 with regard to

1.1 About this Report
This Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG) relates to matters 
arising from performance audits and test audit of transactions of various departments of 
Government of Sikkim pertaining to Social, Economic, Economic (PSUs), Revenue and 
General Sectors and Local Bodies.
The primary purpose of this Report is to bring to the notice of the State Legislature, 
significant results of audit. Auditing standards require that the materiality level for 
reporting should be commensurate with the nature, volume and magnitude of transactions. 
The findings of audit are expected to enable the Executive to take corrective action, 
to frame appropriate policies as well as to issue directives that will lead to improved 
financial management and contribute to better governance. 
This Chapter in addition to explaining the planning and coverage of audit, provides 
a synopsis of significant instances of non-compliance with applicable laws, rules, 
regulations, various orders and instructions issued by competent authorities. 
1.2 Historical Background and Authority for Audit 
Sikkim is the 22 nd State of the Indian Union, having merged with the Indian Union on 
26 April 1975.  Initially, Sikkim Cell was created under the charge of Joint Director, in 
the Office of the Director of Audit, (Central), Kolkata, to discharge the accounting and 
auditing functions for the State of Sikkim. A full-fledged office as an independent unit 
started functioning in Gangtok w.e.f 10 December 1981. Consequent to restructuring of 
cadres in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department on 01 March 1984, this Office was 
bifurcated into two offices, viz., Accounts & Entitlement Office (A&E) and Audit Office. 
Each office is headed by the Accountant General.  
Under the directions of the C&AG, the Office of the Accountant General (Audit), Sikkim 
conducts audit of Government departments, Public Sector Undertakings, Autonomous 
Bodies and other Institutions 1 under Social, Economic, Revenue and General Sectors, 
and Local Bodies which are spread all over the State. The Accountant General (Audit) 
is assisted by a Deputy Accountant General.
The authority for audit is derived from Article 149 and 151 of the Constitution of India 
and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) 
Act, 1971 (C & AG’s (DPC) Act).  Under Section 13 of the C & AG’s (DPC) Act the Office 
of the Accountant General (Audit) has been entrusted with the audit of all expenditure 
incurred from the Consolidated Fund of the Government of Sikkim.  This office conducts 
audit of revenue receipts of the Government of Sikkim under Section 16 of the C&AG’s 
(DPC) Act.  The office of Accountant General (Audit) conducts supplementary audit 
of the accounts of four State Government companies under Section 143 (6) (a) of the 
Companies Act 2013, as these companies are registered under the Companies Act 2013. 
The Companies Act 1956 as well as Companies Act 2013 have not been extended to

1.3 Planning and conduct of Audit
Audit process commences with the assessment of risk of the departments based on the 
expenditure incurred, criticality/complexity of activities, priority accorded for the activity 
by the Government, level of delegated financial powers, assessment of internal controls, 
concerns of stakeholders, previous audit findings, etc. Based on this risk assessment, 
frequency and extent of audit are decided and an annual audit plan is formulated to 
conduct audit. 
After completion of each audit, Inspection Report (IR) containing audit findings is issued 
to the Head of the unit with a request to furnish replies within one month of receipt of 
the IR. Wherever replies are received, audit findings are either settled or further action 
for compliance is advised. Significant audit observations pointed out in these IRs, which 
require attention at the highest level in the Government, are processed for inclusion in 
the Audit Reports which are submitted to the Governor of Sikkim under Article 151 of 
the Constitution of India for being laid in the State Legislature.
Audit Plan is prepared in such a way that it fits into the long term and short-term 
goals of audit in consonance with the overall “Vision and Mission” of the Supreme 
Audit Institution of India.  It is prepared after carrying out risk assessment and 
keeping in view the available manpower. Elements of the Audit Quality Management 
Framework (AQMF) viz., materiality, inputs from V oucher Level Computerisation 
(VLC), financial size of the units, data from various e-Governance initiatives taken by 
government, flagship programmes undertaken by auditees, press criticism/ electronic 
media coverage, expected audit impact and continuous improvement based on past 
experience, etc. are taken into account to the extent possible while framing out the plan. 
A sector wise analysis of government spending, investment policy of the government in 
infrastructure development, industrialisation and socio-economic activities along with 
due consideration of possible audit impact is taken into account in prioritising auditee 
units for preparing the audit plan.
Considering the availability of resources, focus has been given in areas of high financial 
risk than to thinly spreading out resources throughout Government activities. This would 
have better socio-economic impact and add value to governance.  
Out of 1015 auditee units, 266 units were planned for audit during 2022-23 after carrying 
out risk assessment and keeping in view the available human resources, of which 211 
units were actually audited during 2022-23.

2.3.1  Introduction
Government of India (GoI) enacted the Building and Other Construction Workers’ 
(Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996  (BOCW Act) and 

Chapter II: Social Sector
7
Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess Act in 1996  (Cess Act). The 
Acts aimed to provide safety, health, and welfare measures for the benefit of building 
and other construction workers (BOC) through levy/collection of cess.
The Act, inter alia , mandated the constitution of a Building and Other Construction 
Workers’ Welfare Board and framing of rules by every State Government to exercise 
the powers conferred under the Act for the welfare of BOC Workers. The provision of 
the Act applies to “every establishment 2 which employs or had employed on any day 
of the preceding twelve months, ten or more building workers in any building or other 
construction work”. Further, the Act provides that every building worker between the 
age group of 18 to 60  years who was not a member of any welfare fund established 
under any law and had completed ninety days of service during the preceding twelve 
months as a construction worker in the State could be registered as a ‘beneficiary’. 
Government of Sikkim (GoS) notified 3 (August 2010) the Sikkim Building and Other 
Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) (SBOCW) 
Rules, 2010 wherein Rule 263 envisages constitution of fund by the name “The Sikkim 
Building and Other construction Workers Welfare Fund”.  The collection of BOCW 
cess was fixed at the rate of one per cent on the cost of construction incurred by the 
employers. 
The Sikkim Building & Other Construction Workers Welfare Board (SBOCWB) was 
constituted vide State Government notification dated 26 February 20104.
Rule 259 of the SBOCW Rules, 2010 enshrined the powers, duties, and functions of the 
Board as under:
The Board shall be responsible for- 
a) all matters connected with the administration of the fund and grant of benefits to the 
beneficiaries under the Act and Rules made thereof;
b) laying down policies for the deposits of the amount of the fund;
c) submission of an annual budget to the Government on the activities of the Board; 
d) submission of an annual report to the Government on the activities of the Board;
e) proper maintenance of accounts;
f) annual audit of accounts of the Board following the provisions of the Act;
g) collection of contributions to the fund; 
h) launching of prosecution for and on behalf of the Board;
i) speedy settlement of claims and sanction of advances and other benefits;
j) proper and timely recovery of any amount due to the Board, and;
k) submission of information to the Government on such matters as the government 
may refer to it, from time to time.

2.3.8.3 Investment of Welfare Fund in non-nationalised Banks
As per the direction of the Supreme Court (SC)  issued in Writ Petition No. 38 of 
2006 (March 2018), the funds available with the Welfare Boards which have not been 
disbursed or are not likely to be disbursed within a short period should be properly 
invested in nationalised banks only.
Further, section 280 of SBOCW RECS Rules, 2010 specifies investment of cess funds in 
Scheduled banks and Securities under clause (a) to (d) of section 20 of the Indian Trust 
Act, 1882.
Audit observed that during 2017-18 to 2021-22, the Board had invested ₹ 73.44 crore 
in non-nationalised banks11, which was in contravention to the above directions of SC 
and the SBOCW rules, 2010. However, as of March 2022, out of the total investment 
of ₹ 149.41 crore12 the Welfare fund, the Board invested 71.35 per cent of the fund i.e., 
₹ 106.60 crore in non-nationalised banks with only 29 per cent of the investment i.e., 
₹ 42.80 crore having been invested in nationalised banks.
Further, investing welfare funds in non-nationalised banks puts the fund at high risk. 
Since, a welfare fund comprises fee collected for the most vulnerable segment of 
unorganised labour whose works are characterised by their inherent risk to life and 
limbs, complete protection and security of such fund must be ensured by the State for 
keeping it risk-free during any unpredictable financial crisis.

2.3.9  Planning and Implementation of Act
2.3.9.1  Disparity between Act and Government Notification
The Cess Act of 1996, stipulated that proceeds of the cess collected should be paid to the 
Board by the local authority or the State Government collecting the cess after deducting 
cost of collection of cess not exceeding one per cent  of the amount collected. This 
included the cess collected in respect of Government works as well as Private works 
where cess may be collected in advance by the plan-approving authority.
However, the notification issued (September 2010)  by the State Government did not 
include any clause for advance cess collection by building planning authority and one 
per cent collection charges for the service rendered. Further, the notification included 
cess deduction towards construction works of the State Government Departments and it 
did not include the provision of cess deduction from Private constructions (Paragraph 
2.3.11.4). Thus, there was a disparity between the provisions of the Cess Act and the 
State Government notification.
Objective 2: Whether there was an effective system for the registration of 
establishments and beneficiaries?
2.3.10   Implementation of Acts & Rules
2.3.10.1 Registration of BOC Workers
Section 12 of the BOCW Act  and Rule 264 of SBOCW Rules  outline the eligibility 
criteria for registration of a BOC Worker as a beneficiary under the Act. The provisions 
state that any building worker who is between 18 and 60 years of age and had engaged 
in building or construction work for at least 90 days in the preceding 12 months is 
eligible for registration. The registration was a one-time process based on which a 
building worker registered as a beneficiary becomes entitled to the benefits provided by 
the Board from its welfare fund.
Rule 265 of SBCOW Rules, 2010 envisages that an application (Form XXVII) should 
be submitted by the beneficiary to the Beneficiary Registering Officer authorised by the 
Board, with the application form to contain the name of the builder worker, father’s name, 
date of birth, permanent address, marital status, name of the bank, etc. accompanied by 
three passport size photographs and attested copies of the school certificate and birth 
certificate. Thereafter, (Rule 266) on receipt of the application, Registering Officer shall 
register the name of the worker as beneficiary under the Act, provided the applicant has 
complied with all the requirements as laid down in the Rules. Further, Rule 266(4) of 
the SBCOW Rules specifies filing of nomination Form XXXI by the building workers.
Moreover, Section 16 of the BOCW RECS Act 1996 read with Rule 267 (1) of Sikkim 
BOCW Rules 2010 stipulates that a beneficiary of the fund shall contribute to the fund at

₹ 20 per month. This contribution shall be remitted once in 3 months in any of the banks 
specified by the Board in the district in which the member resides.
Further, GoI direction on Model Welfare Scheme envisages that the authority responsible 
for registration of migrant workers must share information with the respective State 
Welfare Board, so that their registration/renewal/delivery of welfare benefits is monitored 
by the Boards of the source States.
Audit observed that the Board had not maintained details of workers viz., name, contact 
numbers, Certificate for age proof and address proof, Bank details, family details for 
nomination, etc. which were required to be submitted by the employer on the above-
prescribed forms. It was only during the audit that the Board provided (31 October 
2022) a list of 5,278 registered workers 13 by considering the contribution/subscription 
fees (September 2022) received from various employers. The Board also could not 
produce a year-wise list of registered workers for the period 2017-22. In the absence of 
such vital data, audit could not ascertain the eligibility of registered workers, yearwise 
trends of registration of workers and could not verify details such as number of workers 
working in the State, since when working, employers under whom they were working, 
etc. in the State.
The Board did not conduct any inspections of the newly registered establishments to 
ensure that eligible workers get registered as ‘beneficiaries’. Also, there was no initiative 
taken by the Board to enrol new BOC workers by conducting awareness programmes as 
elaborated in Paragraph 2.3.13.3 nor was there any initiatives to simplify the process 
of registration for workers, such as through online registration systems. This was also 
evident from the fact that a significant number of construction workers were not found to 
be registered with the Board during JPV . The Board also did not maintain records i.e., the 
certificate of employment issued by the employer to the registered construction workers 
to ensure eligibility to become beneficiaries of BOCW welfare scheme notified by the 
Board. Neither had the Board maintained any records of registered migrant workers, 
nor had they initiated any provision for capturing the change in employer of existing 
registered workers.
Thus, the Board did not have a comprehensive database of the construction workers. 
The Board also could not make satisfactory efforts to enrol unregistered workers. In 
absence of such efforts, there was possibility that eligible workers remained outside the 
ambit of the Act.
2.3.10.2 Non-identification of unregistered establishments

employs, or had employed on any day of the preceding twelve months, ten or more

work, would make an application to the registering officer for registration of the 
establishment within 60 days from the commencement of the work. Also, Chapter IV of 
the SBOCW Rules specifies the manner of registration of the establishments.
Further, Section 43 of the BOCW Act  inter alia stipulates that an Inspector may enter 
any premises or place where building or other construction works are carried on for 
the purpose of examining any records and require the production thereof for inspection

2.3.10.3 Registration of ineligible beneficiaries led to irregular expenditure of ₹ 2.12 
crore
Section 2 (1) (d) of the BOCW Act defines a building or other construction work.  
Further, Section 2(e) of the Act defines a building worker as a person who is employed 
to do any skilled, semi-skilled or unskilled, manual, supervisory, technical or clerical 
work on hire or reward, whether the terms of employment be expressed or implied, in 
connection with any building or other construction work. No workers beyond the ambit 
of the Act should be included or registered under the class of BOC workers.
Scrutiny of records (2017- 22) of registered beneficiaries under the Board showed that 
222 tea plantation workers  from Temi Tea Estate (TTE) were registered by the Board 
as beneficiaries. It was found that the Board had transferred ₹ 1.56 crore  towards  
construction of a creche waiting shed and Badminton court to TTE (2018-19) which was 
not related to the scope of welfare of BOC workers. Further, the Board had also spent 
₹ 4.44 lakh17 as financial relief during COVID-19 (April 2020) and purchased welfare 
items to the tune of ₹ 51.70 lakh (October 2020) for distribution to TTE workers on eight 
occasions (2017-21).
The plantation workers were regular wage earners who were exclusively involved in 
growing and manufacturing tea and were not engaged in any construction activities. 
The plantation workers were governed by the Plantation Labour Act, 1951 and as such 
did not fall under the purview of the BOCW Act. Hence, the registration of 222 plantation 
workers was ineligible and they were not entitled for benefit from the BOCW Welfare 
fund.
Similarly, the Board had also registered workers of Roads and Bridges Department 
(RBD), appointed by the State’s Public Works Department (PWD). The inclusion of 
these workers contradicted the purpose of the BOCW Act, which is intended to protect 
vulnerable workers in temporary and unorganised sectors, as emphasised in the Supreme 
Court’s judgment (March 2018).
The matter of including Muster Roll workers of the PWD under SBOCWB was brought 
to the attention of the Law Department by the Board. The Law Department stated 
(September 2013) that the services of Muster Roll workers under PWD, despite being 
temporary, eventually become regularised by the State and hence could not be brought 
under the ambit of the BOCW Act. This information was communicated during the 14th 
Board Meeting (October 2013) where no decision was given. However, disregarding 
the clear direction from the Law Department, the Board in 32nd Board Meeting (August 
2018) decided to register RBD workers, including those on muster roll and one-family-
one-job basis, under the BOCW Act and transferred ₹ 35.92 lakh during COVID-19 
(March 2020) to the employers bank account for onward transmission to 1796 workers.
As the BOCW Act specifically aimed to meet the welfare of those categories of 
workers who are involved exclusively in Building or other construction works and are 
characterised by their casual nature and temporary relationship with their employer, the 
decision of the Board to incur expenditure for the welfare of tea plantation and PWD 
workers contravened the essence of the Act.
Thus, the expenditure of ₹ 2.48 crore18 from the BOCW Welfare Fund was irregular.

2.3.10.4 Identity Cards (ID Cards) for BOCW beneficiaries 
Section 12 of the BOCW Act  inter alia stipulates that every building worker who has 
completed either 18 years of age, b ut has not completed 60 years of age, and who has 
been engaged in any building or other construction work for not less than ninety days 
during the preceding twelve months shall be eligible for registration as a beneficiary 
under this Act. 
Section 13(I) of the BOCW Act  stipulates that the Board shall issue an identity card 
(ID) to every beneficiary with a photograph duly affixed thereon with enough space for 
entering the details of the building or other construction work done by him/her.
Similarly, Rule 266 (1) of SBOCW Rules  specifies that the Beneficiary Registering 
Officer after receiving the application under Rule 265 shall register the name of the 
worker as a beneficiary under the Act, if such applicant workman has complied with 
all the requirements as laid down in these rules and shall issue an ID card with his 
photograph duly affixed thereon in form XXVIII. Further, it is also stated in the Rule that 
Beneficiary Registering Officer shall maintain a register of ID card issued (Form XXIX).
Scrutiny of records (2017-22) showed that the Board had expended an amount of 
₹ 5.76 lakh19 (March 2019) towards the printing of 5,000 ID cards for issuing to BOC 
Workers. Records showed that these ID cards had been issued to the employers. However, 
there was no record that the BOC workers had received any ID cards. The matter was 
also discussed with the Board during an entry conference (September 2022) wherein it 
was informed that identity cards were issued in all four districts except East. However, 
the Board could not produce records of their issuance such as acknowledgement 
indicating receipt of IDs by the registered workers, register of issued IDs maintained by 
the registering officer, etc. Apart from the above, during the Joint Physical Verification 
of registered establishments and beneficiary survey in selected districts conducted by the 
audit team along with the Board Officials, none of the registered workers or beneficiaries 
could produce any ID card despite being registered with the Board.
The ID card serves as documentary proof that the worker had engaged in construction 
work for more than 90 days to be eligible for registration and availing benefits under 
the Act. However, non-issuance of ID cards was not only in contravention to the above 
Act & Rule but also raises doubts about the genuineness of BOC workers. Further, there 
were no records of receipt of ID cards maintained by the Board which made the entire 
expenditure of ₹ 5.76 lakh for payment against printing of ID cards doubtful.

2.3.10.6  Non-submission of returns by the registered establishments
As per Rule 268 of the SBOCW Rules, 2010  every employer shall before the 15 th day 
of every month submit returns showing the details of workers entitled to be registered 
as well as those who left the service during the preceding month and particulars of the 
establishment. Similarly, as per Rule 242 of the BOCW Rules 1998, every employer 
shall send annually a return relating to an establishment to the Registering Officer having 
jurisdiction ensuring it is received not later than 15 th February following each calendar 
year.
Audit scrutiny showed that none of the employers carrying out building or other 
construction works under the Board’s record had furnished requisite returns during 2017-
22. Resultantly, the Board had no information about the details of the workers entitled 
to be registered, information about the maximum number of building workers employed 
on any day during the year, the total number of days of engagement of building workers, 
etc.
2.3.10.7 Intimation of notice of commencement and completion of the building and 
other construction work
Rule 237 (1) of the SBOCW Rules 2010 stipulates that every employer shall, at least 
thirty days before the commencement of any building or other construction work under 
his control, sent or cause to be sent to the Inspector having jurisdiction, a written notice 
intimation of the actual date of the commencement, the probable date of completion and 
other such particulars as referred to in sub section (1) of section 46 of the Act relating to 
such building or other construction work in Form-IV , annexed to these rules.
Further, as per Section 48 of the BOCW Act, an employer who fails to give notice of the 
commencement of the building or other construction work, shall be punishable with 
imprisonment for a term that may extend to three months, or with a fine that may extend 
to two thousand rupees or both.
Audit observed from records made available that none of the registered establishments 
had intimated the actual date of commencement and probable date of completion as 
per the provision of the Act, ibid. Neither had the Board taken any steps to acquire

failed to provide such notice.
Thus, non-obtaining of information from employers had led to the Board’s inability to 
conduct inspections and identify potential establishments for registration. Consequently,

Objective 3: Whether cess assessment, cess collection and transfer of collected cess 
to the fund were efficient?
During the period 2017-18 to 2021-22, the Board had collected a total cess of ₹ 87.92 crore 
and accumulated interest of ₹ 31.50 crore as exhibited in Table 2.3. Audit noticed various 
deficiencies in collection of cess which includes non-implementation of cess collection 
from Private institutions, absence of well-functioning assessment mechanism and short 
realisation of cess, which has largely affected potential cess receivables in the State as 
elaborated in succeeding paragraphs.
2.3.11 Assessment and Collection of the Cess
2.3.11.1 Non-assessment of cess receivable
Section 4 (1) of the BOCW Act, 1996 stipulates that “Every employer shall furnish such 
return to such officer or authority, in such manner and at such time as may be prescribed”. 
Section 4 (2), further, states that “If any person carrying on building or other construction 
work, liable to pay the cess, fails to furnish any return under subsection (1), the officer or 
the authority shall give a notice requiring such person to furnish such return before such 
date as may be specified in the notice”.
Further, Section 5 of the Act specifies the manner of assessment of cess by the authority 
after making such inquiry, if he thinks fit, from the furnished returns vis-à-vis Section 
4 (1) of the Act and finally, passing of assessment order stipulating specified time on 
which cess shall be paid by the employer.
From records made available, Audit observed that the system of cess assessment and 
passing of assessment orders  not brought into effect although the State had appointed 
ALC/DLC as Assessing Officer (June 2009) for this purpose. Also, the Board did 
not ensure furnishing of returns from the Employers as envisaged in the above Act. 
On its part, the Board only considered the collection of one per cent cess from every 
construction work bill which was received from the employer for obtaining a Labour 
Clearance Certificate (LCC)20. 
Further, the inspection of work sites was also not conducted by any authorised officer 
for verifying the cost of construction. As a result, the overall cost of construction and 
cess to be realised could not be ascertained from scrutiny of records made available 
to Audit.  Thus, there was no scope for assessing the quantum of un-realised cess, 
penalty, or interest. The Board’s approach is fraught with the risk of short collection or 
nonrealisation of the cess which have been illustrated in the succeeding paragraphs.
2.3.11.2 Non-receipt of Cess fund ₹ 2.64 crore
Section 3 to 5 of the Cess Act, 1996 envisages the function of the Board on the collection 
of cess at the rate of one per cent of the cost of construction, furnishing return of the 
employer carrying BOC work, assessment of the cess from the furnished return and

employer. Similarly, Section 4 and 5 of the Cess Rule, 1998 stipulates the manner of cess 
collection and transfer of cess by the Government office, PSUs, and Local authorities 
within 30 days of its collection.
To implement Cess Act in Sikkim, the State vide notification dated 06 September 2010 
directed all the State Government Departments to deduct one per cent cess from the 
estimated cost of construction and forward the same vide Account payee cheque/ Bank

2.3.11.4     Non-collection of advance cess from Private Constructions
The definition of establishment as per Section 2(a)(j) of the BOCW Act, 1996 specifies 
any establishment belonging to, or under the control of Government, corporate or firm, 
an individual or association or other body of individuals which or who employs building 
workers in any building or other construction work; and includes an establishment 
belonging to a contractor, but does not include an individual who employs such workers 
in any building or contraction work concerning his residence the total cost of such 
construction not being more than rupees ten lakh.  Also, Section 1 (4) of the BOCW Act 
states that the Act applies to every establishment which employs, or had employed on 
any day of the preceding twelve months, ten or more building workers in any buildings 
or other construction works.
Section 3(2) of the Cess Act, 1996 specifies a collection of one per cent cess from every 
employer in such manner and at such time, including deduction at source concerning a 
building or other construction work of a Government or of a public sector undertaking 
or advance collection through a local authority where approval of such building or other 
construction work by such local authority is required, as may be prescribed.
Further, as per Section 3(3) “the proceeds of the cess collected under sub-section (2) 
shall be paid by the local authority or the State Government collecting the cess to the 
Board after deducting the cost of collection of such cess not exceeding one per cent of 
the amount collected”.
The above Act stipulates the collection of advance cess by the building plan approval 
authority, which can be achieved by assessing the construction cost outlined  in 
the submitted building plans. The cost of construction of the building area could be 
determined using the plinth area rates set by the State Public Works Department (PWD). 
Subsequently, the planning authority should collect the applicable cess based on the 
calculated construction cost while approving these building plans.
During the period April 2021-December 2022, Gangtok Municipal Corporation (GMC) 
approved 419 building plans in respect of construction works executed by private parties. 
It was observed that the State had not notified the building plans approval authority 
for collection of advance cess from the estimate of construction of the building plan 
as envisaged in Section 3 (2) of the Cess Act. Consequently, in none of the private 
construction works, was applicable advance cess collected and received by the Board. 
Similarly, Urban Development Department (UDD) had approved 15 building plans (Non-
residential/ Commercial buildings) during 2019-22 without commensurate/ applicable 
cess being received by the Board. Also, the Board had also not ventured to register the 
eligible private establishments by conducting inspections as mentioned in preceding 
Paragraphs 2.3.10.1 and 2.3.10.2.
As per the provisions of the Act, the department could have empowered the Local 
Authorities (Municipal Corporation, Panchayats)/Urban Development authorities to

2.3.12.1 Inspection of Building and other construction sites
According to Rule 286 of the SBOCW Rules 2010, an Inspector may, inter alia, examine 
construction site, place, or premises used for a building or other construction work. He 
may issue a show-cause notice or warning to employers regarding the safety, health 
or welfare of building workers provided under the Act or the Rules. Further, he may 
hold an enquiry into the cause of any accident or dangerous occurrence due to any 
operation connected with or incidental to such building or other construction work, or 
of non-compliance with any of provisions of the Act and Rules and give directions in 
this regard.
The Act also aimed at regulating the safety, health, welfare and other conditions of 
service of Building and Other Construction Workers through the Board in every State. 
Sections 32 to 34 of the Act and Rule 241 of the SBOCW Rules, 2010 made it mandatory 
for employers to ensure drinking water, latrines and urinals and accommodation for 
workers. Further, Rule 5 (9) of the SBOCW Rules, 2010 mandates maintenance of clean 
and hygienic condition of latrines and urinals by the employers.
It was observed that the Board (2017-22) had not conducted any inspections for ensuring 
health and safety measures despite incurring expenditure of ₹ 27.02 lakh for this purpose, 
as there were no records of conducted inspections i.e., inspection reports, inspection 
notes, etc. during the audit period.
Joint Physical Verification (JPV) of 16 construction sites (eight registered and eight 
unregistered establishments from two selected Districts) with the Board Officials showed 
instances of non-availability of basic amenities as detailed in Paragraph 2.3.16.

2.3.13.2 Non-implementation of group insurance to BOC Workers
Section 22(d) of the BOCW (RECS) Act 1996 envisages the implementation of a Group 
Insurance scheme for registered workers. This had also been reiterated in the Model 
Welfare Scheme by GoI according to which the State Welfare Board should cover BOC 
workers between the ages 18 to 50 years  under Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima 
Yojana (PMJJBY) and Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY).
The Board in its 38thmeeting (January 2020) discussed the implementation of the scheme, 
however, audit observed that no concrete steps had been taken to implement the scheme.
2.3.13.3  Lack of awareness among BOC Workers
The direction issued by the Supreme Court (18 January 2010),  inter alia,  stated that 
awareness should be built up, about the registration of building workers and about the 
benefits available under the Act. There should be an effective use of media, AIR and 
Doordarshan, for awareness programmes regarding the Act, the benefits available there 
and procedures for availing the benefits.
Further, under the directions (March 2018) of the Supreme Court, the MoL&E, GoI 
had prepared Model Scheme for BOC Workers and Action Plan (for Strengthening 
Implementation Machinery). This included awareness generation among BOC workers.
Audit revealed that the Board incurred an expenditure of ₹ 35.04 lakh 29  (2017-22) for 
organising various awareness programmes. However, records of conducted programmes 
were not produced to audit.
This is, further, substantiated by the fact that an extremely smaller number of beneficiaries 
(61 claims) had availed the scheme benefits (2017-22). It was also noticed during the 
beneficiary survey that 85 out of 158 selected workers were unaware of the Board and 
its projected welfare schemes, which was reflective of the alarmingly low figure of 
registered BOC workers i.e., 5,278 in the State (October 2022).

2.3.13.5 Excess procurement of welfare items- ₹ 1.72 crore
Department of Labour, Government of Sikkim vide notification no. 06/DL dated 
12 March 2015 framed 22 schemes which included schemes for distribution of Welfare 
items i.e., Blankets, boots, shoes, tools, etc. for the BOC workers. The State framed the 
above scheme in the exercise of the power conferred under clause (h) of section 22 (1) 
of the BOCW Act, 1996. Accordingly, the Board during the period 2017-18 to 2018-19 
decided to implement distribution of welfare items on numerous occasions and the same 
was approved during the Board meetings.
Audit observed that during 2017-18 to 2019-20, on four occasions, the Board incurred 
an expenditure of ₹ 8.91 crore for the purchase of welfare  items35 for distribution to 
potential beneficiaries. It was, however, noticed that the Board had procured welfare 
items by estimating a higher number 36 of registered workers even though the active 
beneficiaries during that period were comparatively less in number (Appendix 2.7).  
Audit found that an excess of 5,121 welfare items was procured which had resulted in an 
unwarranted expenditure of ₹ 1.72 crore from the Welfare fund. Records indicating the 
availability/utilisation of these items were not made available to Audit. It was observed 
that the Board had not maintained the list of registered beneficiaries and had relied on 
the provisional figures of registered workers taken from the establishments at the time 
of scheme implementation. Further, the distribution of the excess items to ineligible 
persons cannot be ruled out.
Thus, the inability of the Board to assess the actual number of beneficiaries before 
procurement of welfare items and the lack of records indicating the existence of the 
excess purchased items resulted in a wasteful expenditure of ₹ 1.72 crore from the 
welfare fund.

2.3.18 Conclusion
The Sikkim Building and Other Construction Welfare Board was established to 
ensure the safety and welfare of construction workers. Audit observed deficiencies in 
the implementation of the BOCW Act and related rules in the state of Sikkim which 
included non identification of establishments for registration (Paragraph 2.3.10.2) , 
inability to assess and collect the cess (Paragraph 2.3.11.1 and 2.3.11.2), non-conduct 
of inspection at sites (Paragraph 2.3.12.1)  and improper implementation of welfare 
schemes (Paragraph 2.3.13.1). 
The Board had neither initiated a proper system of registering establishments/workers 
nor established a sound assessment mechanism for collecting cess. There was no 
mechanism for online registration of the establishments and workers as of date. As a 
result, the Board was unaware about the exact number of construction workers in the 
state as evidenced by the differing figures produced by the Board on different occasions. 
This also indicated that the Board was not aware of the exact quantum of cess due for 
collection and that the estimation of beneficiaries for various welfare schemes was not 
realistic. 
The Board did not have independent staff of its own, and its day-to-day activities were 
managed by the staff of the labour department itself, in addition to their normal work 
and duties. Audit observed that this had resulted in the improper implementation of the 
BOCW act. Critical activities such as inspection of establishments, ensuring submission 
of mandatory returns by employers and maintenance of records were not done properly 
by the Board. Further, Audit also noticed instances where cess funds were diverted to 
activities not related to BOCW.
Audit noticed that the expenditure on various welfare activities is very low as compared 
with the total accumulated cess funds available with the Board. This translated into 
very few beneficiaries receiving financial assistance from the Board. Further, there were 
instances of beneficiaries being provided financial assistance after a considerable delay. 
Audit also noticed that employers had failed to promptly report incidents/accidents 
which happened at the work sites and necessary action was not taken action by the 
Board in this regard. Apart from these, Audit further noticed that awareness regarding 
welfare schemes under the Act was low amongst the workers. 
Audit concludes that the SBOCW Board has remained ineffective in executing the 
provisions of the BOCW act for the welfare of construction workers of the State of 
Sikkim. 
2.3.19 Recommendations
For better and more effective implementation of the act, it is recommended that –
	The Board shall ensure the preparation and submission of the Annual Budget for 
approval of the Government.
	The Government should ensure that the Cess Fund is used exclusively for the welfare 
measures of the BOC workers only. The use of funds for administrative purposes 
should be within the permissible limit of five per cent of total expenditure.

	Online registration mechanism for BOC workers with complete details (name, 
contact number, nominees, bank details, identification documents, subscription fee, 
etc.) is to be initiated by the Board at the earliest. Further, the Board should ensure 
that all construction works and workers involved are registered under the Board. 
The Board should maintain a comprehensive database of such registered workers.
	The Board should institutionalise a mechanism to identify all employers and 
workers and ensure proper and timely collection of cess.
	The Board may ensure that Assessment Officers and Cess collectors are made 
accountable for ensuring that the cess is duly assessed, realised and remitted to the 
Board.
	The Government may authorise the advance collection of cess from Private

	The Government should ensure investing the Cess fund in nationalised banks only.
	Transit accommodation/hostel/ labour shed/ night shelter for the BOC workers

	The Government may ensure mandatory provision of financial assistance through

2.4.1  Introduction
The public healthcare delivery system in India is organised at three levels – primary, 
secondary, and tertiary. The vast network of Primary Health Sub-Centres (SCs), Primary 
Health Centres (PHCs), Urban Primary Health Centres (UPHCs) and Community Health 
Centres (CHCs) form the primary tier of public healthcare delivery system for rural and 
urban population. District Hospitals (DHs) provide secondary-level healthcare services 
for rural and urban population. These hospitals handle the treatment and management of 
diseases or medical conditions that require specialised care. Tertiary healthcare involves 
providing advanced and super-specialty services to be provided by medical institutions 
in urban areas, which are well-equipped with sophisticated diagnostic and investigative 
facilities. 
2.4.2 Overview of Public Healthcare facilities in Sikkim
Sikkim is the least populated and second smallest State in India with a population of 
6.83 lakh (2021-22). To provide universal healthcare services to the people, the State 
has a 1000 bedded Super Specialty Hospital at Gangtok, four District Hospitals, two 
Community Health Centres (CHCs), two Ayush Hospitals, one TB Hospital, one Covid 
Hospital, 24 Primary Health Centres (PHCs), two Urban Primary Health Centres 
(UPHCs) and 148 Public Health Sub-Centres (PHSCs). 
Analysis of the existence of health centres in the State at the primary and secondary 
levels vis-à-vis the norm laid down by the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) for a 
hilly/mountainous State revealed the availability of an adequate number of DHs4546

District Hospitals provide IPD Services in Medicine, Surgery, Maternity, Paediatrics, 
Nursery, Isolation related cases, Burn cases, Orthopaedics, Ophthalmology, Malaria and

The four District Hospitals of Sikkim provided IPD Services based on availability of 
Specialist Doctors with each Hospital. Maximum in-patients in the DHs pertained to

2.4.8 Availability of Diagnostic Service in the District Hospitals
According to the IPHS, the District Hospital laboratory and other diagnostic services 
shall serve the purpose of public health and be able to perform all tests required to 
diagnose epidemics or important diseases.  The Laboratory services which are to be 
available in a District Hospital are i) Clinical Pathology ii) Pathology iii) Microbiology

2.4.12 Ambulance Service 
In terms of the IPHS (Clause XVI Hospital Transport Services) norms, a District Hospital 
shall have well equipped Basic Life Support (BLS) and desirably one Advanced Life 
Support (ALS) ambulance. 
The NHM guidelines prescribe the availability of tele-ambulance services which can be 
availed by calling telephone numbers 108 and 102 for attending to patients of critical 
care, trauma (accident) victims etc., (108) and basic patient transport to cater to the 
needs of pregnant women, children etc. (102).  
Audit noticed that there were 13 ambulances in four DHs of the State (Singtam DH- four; 
Namchi DH- four; Geyzing DH – three & Mangan DH - two) . The DHs provided free 
ambulance service as referral transport to higher health facilities. The ambulances were 
provided with basic life support facility viz., Oxygen Cylinder, First Aid Box, trained 
paramedics, etc. as required under the IPHS norms. However, only one ambulance under 
Geyzing DH in West district was connected with 102 national ambulance service catering 
to pregnant women, sick infants and sterilisation cases while ‘108 Emergency Transport 
System’ service for all other medical emergencies was not available in the State.  
2.4.13 Good practices 
The following good practices were noticed in the District Hospitals of the State: 
➢ Management of Bio Medical Waste 
Biomedical waste management (BMW) is an integral part of infection control activities 
of the hospital. According to the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (BMW 
Rules) hazardous, toxic and bio-medical waste has to be separated into 10 categories 
for the purpose of safe transportation to specific sites for specific treatment. Further, the 
BMW Rules inter alia stipulate the procedures for collection, handling, transportation, 
disposal and monitoring of the bio-medical Waste with clear roles for waste generators.
Audit noticed that all four DHs were segregating hospital wastes in separate-coloured 
bins, available at the point of generation of waste, particularly in the ward areas, OTs, 
etc. as per the BMW rules. Incinerators were available in all four DHs for burning of 
the BMW and deep burial pits (sharp pits) were available for burial of sharp objects 
calling for such burial. General solid wastes were collected by the concerned municipal 
authorities for disposal while recyclable items were handed over to agencies collecting 
such items. 
➢ Mortuary Service in the District Hospitals
IPHS provides that every District Hospital should have the facilities for keeping of dead 
bodies and conducting autopsy.
Audit noticed that all the DHs in the State had a mortuary service for keeping the dead 
bodies and conducting of autopsy as per norms. 
2.4.14 Status of Implementation of AB-PMJAY in Sikkim 
Ayushman Bharat- Pradhan Mantri Jan Aarogya Yojana ( AB-PMJAY) is a flagship 
health scheme of the GoI, launched (23 September 2018) to achieve Universal Health 
Coverage (UHC) as recommended in the National Health Policy, 2017. PM -JAY aims 
to provide health insurance cover of ₹ five lakh per family per year for secondary and 

Chapter II: Social Sector
43
tertiary care hospitalisation.  Under PMJAY , the States are free to choose the modalities 
of implementation of the Scheme.  State can implement the scheme through insurance 
company or directly through the Trust / Society or mixed model. Sikkim chose to 
implement the PMJAY Scheme in trust mode where a Government of India (GoI) 
empanelled Third Party Agency (TPA) was appointed to support implementation of the 
Scheme. 
The scheme was rolled out in the State on the same day it was launched nationally 
(23 September 2018).  State Empanelment Committee (SEC) was formed on 06 February 
2023 with the objective of providing requisite support and physical verification of the 
health facilities for their empanelment under the AB-PMJAY . District Implementation 
Units (DIUs) were simultaneously set up in four districts (East District, West District, 
North District and South District) with the objective of supporting implementation of 
the Scheme in each district included under the Scheme. Further, 801 Contact points were 
established at district, sub-division and block levels for registration of beneficiaries.  
All the empanelled hospitals also had beneficiary registration facilities. The State had 
empanelled 17 hospitals (16 public hospitals and one private hospital) as of March 2022.
On being pointed out about delay in establishment of SEC, the Department stated that 
the delay was due to existence of a standing Hospital Empanelment Committee since 
August 2018 which performed the functions of the SEC.
As per Socio Economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011, there were 1.39 lakh members 
of 39,791 distinct households in the State eligible for availing benefits under the AB-
PMJAY scheme. However, as of 31 March 2022, only 0.45 lakh (32 per cent) members 
of 14,966 (38 per cent) households had been registered. A total of 5198 beneficiaries 
had been admitted under the scheme in various hospitals of the State during 2018-22 
against whom claims amounting to ₹ 3.01 crore had been paid by Government to various 
hospitals during the period.
2.4.15 Operationalisation of Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) 
Government of India announced (February 2018) creation of 1.50 lakh Health and Wellness 
Centres (HWCs) by transforming existing Sub Centres and Primary Health Centres 
as the base pillar of Ayushman Bharat. These centres would deliver Comprehensive 
Primary Health Care (CPHC) bringing healthcare closer to homes of people covering 
both maternal and child health services and non-communicable diseases, including free 
essential drugs and diagnostic services. 
In Sikkim, all 26 Primary Health Centres (PHCs/UPHCs) and 144 Public Health Sub 
Centres (PHSCs) have been transformed (March 2023) into Health and Wellness Centres 
(HWCs) as envisaged by the Government of India. A total of 5.17 lakh patients in the 
State had been served by the HWCs as of March 2023.
