consumables may be made from the SIMFED 58 on the plea that it was difficult to call 
fresh tenders due to the lock-down.  Audit noticed that Quotations from SIMFED were 
invited in June 2020 and supply orders for the medicines and consumables were issued 
to SIMFED in August 2020 and September 2020 respectively for ₹ 40 crore and the 
supplies were completed by March 2021.  
It may be mentioned that SIMFED had not been authorised by the State Government in 
its allocation of business to supply medicines and medical consumables to the H&FW 
Department. It was also unclear as to how the Department presumed SIMFED would be 
able to supply medicines and consumables at reasonable rates promptly during lockdown 
without calling for competitive bids. 
Thus, despite having valid tendered rates, the Department’s decision to procure 
medicines and consumables from SIMFED, despite SIMFED not being authorised to 
supply medical items, on the plea of inability to call fresh tenders due to lockdown, was 
irregular. 
Audit noticed that out of 237 items purchased from SIMFED, 19 items were purchased 
at rates equal to the tendered rates, 42 items at rates slightly lower than the tendered rates 
leading to saving of ₹ 27.39 lakh and 176 items at much higher rates leading to excess 
expenditure of ₹ 2.93 crore. Thus, there was net excess expenditure of ₹  2.66 crore 
from the public exchequer on purchase of medical items from SIMFED, despite the 
Department having valid lower tendered rates.
2.4.22.6 Conclusion
●	 The State had neither formulated its Health Policy nor did it adhere to the NHP 17 
stipulation of allocating adequate funds to the Health Sector. The State’s expenditure 
on health was below two per cent of the GSDP during 2017-22 and fell short of the 
NHP 17 stipulation during the period.  
●	 Shortfall in the allocation/expenditure of funds for health sector as compared to the 
NHP 17 resulted in inability to provide essential specialist services in the two CHCs 
of the State and some vital services in the DHs of North, East and West districts 
like surgery, paediatrics, anaesthesia, ophthalmology, etc. while desirable services, 
which the CHCs and DHs were to aspire for, were missing in all the CHCs and DHs 
of the State. 
●	 The meagre revenue expenditure of 0.11 per cent  for maintenance of health 
infrastructure negatively impacted the upkeep of infrastructure to the required 
standard.  
●	 Rather than increasing funds for repair and maintenance of infrastructure over time, 
the State Government kept downsizing funds, from ₹ 49.37 lakh during 2017-18 to 
₹40.43 lakh during 2021-22.  
●	 There were instances of unwarranted expenditure of ₹ 2.93 crore on procurement of 
medicines and consumables as well as infructuous expenditure of ₹ 6.23 crore on 
construction activities.

(ii)    Antenatal Care
Antenatal care is the systemic supervision of women during pregnancy to monitor the 
progress of foetal growth and to ascertain the well-being of the mother and the foetus. A 
proper antenatal check-up provides necessary care to the mother and helps identify any 
complications of pregnancy such as anaemia, pre-eclampsia, hypertension, etc. 
Antenatal Care (ANC) check-up
As per instructions issued by the Maternal Health Division, Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare, all pregnant women (PW) are required to be registered and minimum 
four Antenatal Care (ANC) check-ups are needed to be conducted. Each pregnant woman 
is given a unique ID while registering her name and details in the Reproductive and 
Child Health (RCH) Register in the facility and is given a Mother and Child Protection 
(MCP) card. All the investigations done and date of visit have to be recorded in the MCP 
card and the same is required to be updated in the RCH Register. All pregnant women 
who are registered with MCP card are to be given Iron Folic Acid (IFA) tablets and 
Calcium tablets compulsorily. IFA tablets (180) have been prescribed for six months 
during pregnancy and are to be continued for six months post-partum.

2.4.23.14  Conclusion
●	 The shortage of PHSCs, PHCs and CHCs in the three districts of the State deprived 
the benefits of proper healthcare facilities from being provided to the rural population 
of the districts near their place of residence.  
●	 OTs in the sampled DHs Singtam & Geyzing suffered from lack of essential 
equipment as well as the specialist doctors in surgery. As a result, the OTs functioned 
only partially for addressing minor surgical procedures. OT in the Rhenock CHC 
also remained non-functional due to non-availability of surgeon and the blood 
storage facility.
●	 Absence of specialist services in the Rhenock CHC deprived sick people of essential 
healthcare services expected from a CHC closer to their homes. 
●	 Deployment of specialists, medical officers, nurses and paramedics in the two 
sampled DHs was done without considering either actual requirement or the IPHS 

Audit Report for the year ended 31 March 2023
64
norm. This resulted in non-availability of services in some Departments while 
leading to underutilisation of manpower in Departments having excess staff. 
●	 The State was experiencing higher still birth rate (percentage) over and above the 
all India average.
●	 There were discrepancies in the figures of total live births, total deliveries and the 
total number of stillbirths captured in the health management information system 
(HMIS) of the Department indicating flaws in the process of data collection and 
data management.
2.3.23.15 Recommendations
i) The Department may take initiative to make good the shortage of essential equipment 
and ensure availability of required specialist services and blood storage facility in 
the OTs of the DHs and CHCs. 
ii) Specialist services viz., Surgery, Medicine, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Paediatrics 
and Anaesthesia, etc. may be introduced in the CHCs in the State as required under 
the IPH norms. 
iii) Specialists, medical officers, nurses and paramedics in the sampled DHs (Singtam 
and Geyzing) may be redeployed based on IPH norms and actual requirement.
iv) Government may take steps to set up new PHSCs, PHCs and CHCs to mitigate the 
shortages (five CHCs, nine PHCs and 67 PHSCs) in the two districts of the State 
and to ensure availability of proper healthcare facilities near the place of residence 
of people of those areas. 
v) The Department may take steps to identify reasons for high stillbirth rates in the 
State and take corrective measures to reduce the rate.
vi) The Department may take steps to ensure robust data entry and validation 
processes.
Objective 3: Whether Support services in the health facilities were available and 
adequate
2.4.24 Other Support Services
The operational activities of a health facility comprise a wide variety of support services 
viz., management of linens, dietary management, ambulance service, sweeping and 
cleaning service, hospital security service, etc. Management of support services in the 
sampled health institutions is discussed in Paragraphs 2.4.24.1 to 2.4.24.6. 
2.4.24.1 Hospital linen services
As per IPHS, the number of linen (OT coats, bed sheets, bed covers, pillows, blankets, 
pillow covers) required in DHs, CHCs & PHCs has been quantified as per the bed 
strength of each health facility.
During physical verification (April 2023), use of hospital issued linens like bed sheets, 
blankets and pillows by the patients was found very rare.  There was no provision for 
providing patient-dresses to the in-patients.  Most of the patients preferred to use their 
own linens and blankets rather than that provided by the hospitals. Washing machines for 
cleaning the hospital linen were available, however, ironing facilities were not available 
in the sampled health facilities.

2.4.24.2 Good Practices in Staff Immunisation and Hospital Disinfection
 Staff	immunisation 
Periodic medical check-up and immunisation of staff is a part of the hospital infection 
control programme and to be followed by the DHs, CHCs and the PHCs as per norms. 
Audit noticed that the sampled health facilities provided Hepatitis B and Tetanus 
injections to all its health care workers and ensured immunisation of staff from infectious 
diseases.  
 Disinfection and sterilisation 
To prevent hospital acquired infections in patients, visitors and staff, the NHM Assessor’s 
Guidebook 2013 required each DH to frame a schedule of procedure to be followed 
by the health care facilities known as Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for septic 
procedures, culture surveillance and determination of hospital acquired infections. The 
facility should also have standard procedures for processing disinfection and sterilisation 
of equipment and instruments.  
Audit observed that both DHs had functional Infection Control Committees headed by 
CMO of the respective DH and had SOPs for septic procedures, culture surveillance and 
determination of hospital acquired infections. The sampled hospitals adopted boiling, 
autoclaving, and chemical sterilisation processes for disinfection and sterilisation of 
hospital equipment and instruments. 
2.4.24.3 Disaster management and fire security
NHM Assessor’s Guidebook envisages that a Disaster Management Plan (DMP) be 
prepared for each health facility. Besides, disaster management training for hospital staff 
and conducting periodic mock drills in the hospitals is necessary. Standard Operating 
Procedures (SOPs) should be available, and a disaster management committee should 
be constituted. 
Audit noticed that the sampled hospitals had disaster management plan but had not 
developed SOPs on disaster management. Mock drills on disaster management and 
fire safety drills were conducted periodically. Though the sampled health facilities had 
adequate number of fire extinguishers, fire detection alarms were not available in any of 
the sampled health centres.  
2.4.24.4 Power back-up and water supply
Physical verification of the sampled units revealed (April 2023) availability of 24x7 
power supply including back-up arrangement in both the DHs. Besides, the DHs also 
had power inverters installed in the Emergency wards and OTs. However, in respect 
of the PHCs, the DG sets provided were functional in only two PHCs ( Sombaria and 
Pakyong) out of the sampled five PHCs. The DG set provided to the CHC Rhenock 
was also non-functional. The DG sets were non-functional due to lack of recharge or 
nonreplacement of the dead batteries used in the DG sets to start. 
Singtam DH had frequent water shortages due to absence of a dedicated supply line 
of water and absence of dedicated maintenance plan and manpower to ensure regular 
upkeep of the water supply system.

2.4.24.5 Ambulance Service
In terms of the IPHS (Clause XVI Hospital Transport Services) norms, a District 
Hospital shall have well equipped Basic Life Support (BLS) and desirably one Advanced 
Life Support (ALS) ambulance. For a DH of bed capacity 101 to 200 beds (Clause-
XIII), availability of three ambulances was prescribed. The NHM guidelines prescribe 
availability of national ambulance services which can be availed by calling telephone 
numbers 108 and 102 for attending to patients of critical care, trauma, and accident 
victims etc. (108) and basic patient transport to cater to the needs of pregnant women, 
children etc. (102).  
Audit noticed that there were three standby ambulances in Geyzing DH for referral 
services in case of emergencies.  These ambulances were fitted with basic life support 
(BLS) system having oxygen support and suction machines. Besides, there were an 
additional seven ambulances in the PHCs of West District which could be availed 
through Call Centre No. 102 for pregnancy related cases.  
Singtam DH had four ambulances with BLS system. Apart from these four ambulances, 
there was at least one ambulance in each of the five PHCs and two ambulances in 
the Rhenock CHC under Singtam DH that were used for transporting patients. The 
ambulances under Singtam DH were, however, not connected with the 102 national 
ambulance service. 
For all other critical cases, 108 connectivity was however not available in the test 
checked health facilities.

2.4.24.7 Assessment of Performance
All the eight hospitals and health centres sampled for Audit had BOR ranging between 
eight to 78 per cent, which was below the IPHS norm of 80 to 100 per cent. Machong 
PHC had the lowest BOR of 8.13 while Rinchengpong PHC had the second lowest 
BOR of 20.04. This was despite these two PHCs having excess manpower (29 and 40) 
in various cadres. Pakyong PHC had highest BOR of 77.31 per cent and lowest referral 
out rate of 76 indicating relatively better patient care and better availability of services 
at that PHC.  All the health centres, excepting Pakyong PHC, had much higher ROR 
which indicated dearth of adequate facilities and services in those centres compelling 
the hospital authorities to refer critical and emergent cases for better medical service 
from elsewhere.  
2.4.24.8 Conclusion
Ambulance service under Call Centre No.102 for pregnancy related cases was available 
only in the West District in the State while the service under call centre No. 108 for other 
emergencies was not available in any of the test checked health facilities. 
2.4.24.9  Recommendations 
i) The Department may take immediate steps to provide dedicated water supply line 
to the Singtam District Hospital and ensure its regular maintenance.
ii) Ambulance service under Call Centre No.102 for pregnancy related cases and 108 
for other emergencies may be made available for all health facilities.

2.4.26.7 Conclusion
●	 The State had established RTPCR testing facility only in the STNM Hospital at 
Gangtok. None of the district hospitals had functioning RTPCR facility during 
2020-22.  
●	 The 50 bedded Covid Hospital at Karfectar remained idle for more than a year 
since its creation in August 2022. The Department / Government had not taken any 
decision to utilise the building.
●	 Out of the six O 2 generating plants having total installed capacity of 3900 lpm set 
up during 2021-22 in the five hospitals in the State, two plants of 1200 lpm set 
up in Mangan and Singtam DH were lying idle due to non-provisioning of DG 
sets while one plant of 1000 lpm installed at the STNM Hospital functioned only 
intermittently.  
●	 A large number of Ventilators (51) and Oxygen concentrators (12) were lying idle 
and unused in the Departmental Stores and the Stores of STNM Hospital  
●	 Despite installation of the oxygen plants and idling of existing oxygen concentrators, 
the dependence on bottled oxygen in the hospitals had not reduced.   
2.4.26.8 Recommendations
i) The Department may make RTPCR cum Virology labs functional in the DHs. 
ii) The Department /Government should prepare an action plan for utilising the 
idle newly constructed 50 bedded Covid Hospital constructed at Karfectar at the 
earliest.
iii) The Department may ensure regular repair and upkeep of the Oxygen generating 
plants with a view to ensure their utility. 
iv) The Department may take stock of the idle ventilators and concentrators in the 
stores and ensure their usage or disposal, as appropriate.

2.4.27.6  Conclusion 
●	 The State was lagging behind in four health indicators in comparison to the National 
average as per the SDG India Index Dash-Board 2021– percentage of immunisation 
of children in the age group 9-11 years, suicide rate; death rate due to road accidents 
and total number of physicians, nurses and midwives per 10000 population.

suicide rate and death due to road accidents.

national average. This was a matter of serious concern for the State Government. 
2.4.27.7 Recommendations

supervision of the health and family welfare programmes with a view to ensure 
achieving the SDG 3 targets.

and deaths due to road accidents in the state and make concerted efforts to contain 
the same.

on expenditure incurred, criticality/complexity of activities, level of delegated financial 
powers, assessment of overall internal controls, etc.
After completion of audit of each unit on a test check basis, Inspection Reports (IRs) 
containing audit findings are issued to the heads of the departments. The departments 
are required to furnish replies to the audit findings within one month of receipt of the 
IRs. Whenever replies are received, audit findings are either settled based on reply/
action taken or further action is required by the audited entities for compliance. Some of 
the important audit observations arising out of these IRs are processed for inclusion in 
the Audit Reports. The Audit Reports are submitted to the Governor of the State under 
Article 151 of the Constitution of India for laying on the table of the Legislature for 
taking further appropriate action.

3.3.1 Introduction
Rural Road Connectivity, and its sustained availability, is a key component to Rural 
Development. Despite rural roads being a state subject and the responsibility of providing 
connectivity to all village/habitations resting with the state governments, the Government 
of India, acknowledging the expected socio-economic benefits to the rural population 
from rural roads and as a strategy for poverty alleviation and to overcome deficiencies in 
rural road planning, introduced (December 2000) a centrally sponsored scheme ‘Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana’  (PMGSY)  to provide all-weather road 6667
68 connectivity 
including necessary bridges to eligible unconnected habitations in rural areas.
The objective of the PMGSY is to provide connectivity, by way of an ‘all-weather road’ 
to the eligible unconnected habitations (Census 2001) in the rural areas with a population 
of 500 persons and above in plain areas and 250 persons in hilly areas.
PMGSY-I was initially a 100 per cent centrally sponsored scheme, but from the year 
2015-16, the funding is shared between the Centre and the State as 90:10 for North 
Eastern and Himalayan States.
As the Programme unfolded, a dire need to consolidate the entire rural road network by 
upgradation69 of selected Through Routes 70 and some Major Rural Links (MRLs) was 
felt and accordingly a new intervention was evolved in May 2013 namely PMGSY-II. 
PMGSY–II envisages consolidation of the existing Rural Road Network by covering 
upgradation of selected rural roads based on their economic potential and their role in 
facilitating the growth of rural market centres and rural hubs.
National Rural Infrastructure Development Agency (NRIDA) was registered (January 
2002) as a society for extending technical and management support to the GoI in 
implementation of PMGSY . 
66 
67 
68  An All Weather Road is one which is negotiable during all weathers, with some permitted interruptions. 
Essentially this means that at cross-drainage structures, the duration of overflow or interruption at 
one stretch shall not exceed 12 hours for ODRs and 24 hours for VRs in hilly terrain, and 3 days in 
the case of roads in plain terrain. The total period of interruption during the year should not exceed 
10 days for ODRs and 15 days for VRs. The pavement should be negotiable during all-weathers, but 
this does not necessarily imply that it should be paved or sealed or blacktopped.
69 Upgradation  shall cover the improvement of surface drainage and constructing all missing cross-
drainage works to make the road all-weather, improvement the road pavement to standards required 
for the traffic, subject to condition and road geometrics to prescribed standards and improving road 
safety.
70 Through Routes  are the roads which collect traffic from several link roads or a long chain of 
Habitations and lead it to Marketing centres either directly or through the higher category roads i.e., 
the District Roads or the State or National Highway.

•The District Rural Roads Plan (DRRP) is a long-term plan of road network in a district,
showing the existing road network, the habitations of various population size and roads
proposed for connecting the yet unconnected habitations to already connected
habitations/ all-weather roads in an economic and efficient way in terms of cost and
utility. It is also known as the Master Plan for Rural Roads for the district.
Core network
•Core Network (CN) : It directly flows from the DRRP. The rural road network
required for providing the ‘basic access’ to all villages/ habitations is termed as the
Core Network. Basic access is defined as one all-weather road access from each
village/ habitation to the nearby Market Centre or Rural Business Hub (RBH) and
essential social and economic services. A Core Network comprises Through Routes
and Link Routes. The Core Network is the only basis for selection of works under
PMGSY.
CNCPL
•Comprehensive New Connectivity Priority List (CNCPL) : Once the Core Network is
ready, the States are required to prepare CNCPL at Block and District level, of all
proposed road links under PMGSY (with road code, names of habitations being
connected with habitations code, population served and length). For a given Order of
Priority and a given planning unit, the listing can be on the basis of total population
benefited.

3.3.9.2 Non-recovery of Liquidated damage 
Clause 44 of Standard Biding Document (SBD) stipulates that one per cent of the initial 
contract price per week would be the amount of Liquidated Damages (LDs) for delay in 
completion subject to a maximum of 10 per cent of the initial contract price.
Examination of records revealed that 37 delayed works were under execution during 
audit period which were sanctioned during 2007-08 to 2021-22. In all these works, RDD 
had attributed the delay to the contractors and had issued notices to them from time to 
time. However, LD at the prescribed rate amounting to ₹ 17.21 crore had not been levied 
on the contractors by invoking Clause 44 of the SBD.

3.3.9.3 Status of equipment advances granted to contractors
Clause 45 of Standard Biding Document stipulates that on the request of the Contractor, 
the Employer will make the following advance payment to the Contractor against 
submission by the Contractor of an Unconditional Bank Guarantee from a scheduled 
Commercial bank acceptable to the Employer in amounts equal to 110 per cent of the 
amount of the advance payment being requested: 
a. Mobilisation advances up to five per cent of the initial contract price excluding the 
contract price for routine maintenance 
b. Equipment Advance up to 90 per cent of the cost of the new equipment brought to 
the site, subject to a maximum of 10 per cent of the initial contract price excluding 
the contract price for routine maintenance
The Bank Guarantee shall remain effective until the advance payment has been repaid, 
but the amount of the guarantee shall be progressively reduced by the amounts repaid 
by the contractors. Interest will not be charged on the advance payment. However, if the 
Contract is terminated due to default of the Contractor, the Mobilisation Advance and 
the Equipment Advance shall be deemed to be an interest bearing advance at the base 
rate of the State Bank of India, from the date of such advance payment. 
Further, the Contractor is to use the advance payment only to pay for Equipment, 
plant and Mobilisation expenses required specifically for execution of the Works and

PMGSY is to provide good all weather road connectivity to the eligible unconnected 
habitations”. Further, as per PMGSY scheme guidelines para 8.5 (VI b), the habitation 
concerned will not be counted as “connected” till the second stage is taken up. 
The Indian Road Congress (IRC) Hill Roads Manual stipulates the following: The water 
courses and high intensity of rainfall calls for effective drainage of roads which causes 
problems like soft surfaces, potholes, rutting, washout shoulders and even failure of 
complete section of roadway structures. Prevention of such failures requires good degree

up hill slopes along a road are termed as Breast Wall for protection against instability at 
places from failing by slumping, sliding, toe failure.

drainage structure and protective wall should be suitably incorporated in the DPR by 
concerned PIUs based on site requirement of the rural roads to achieve the objective 
of PMGSY . Further, in ongoing works, routine maintenance work such as clearance of

3.3.10.10 Non-provision of insurance cover
According to Paragraph 9.3.1 of the Operations Manual and Clause 13.1 of General 
Conditions of Contract (GCC), the contractor at his cost shall provide all risk insurance 
cover in the joint name of the Employer and the Contractor on the amount of full contract 
price in the Contract Data. The insurance shall be effective from the start date, up to 
the date of actual completion of the work. The scope of the insurance shall cover fire, 
lightning, explosion, impact, flood, inundation, storm, earthquake, subsidence, landslide, 
theft, burglary, R&S and terrorist damage. Lack of insurance cover is a fundamental 
breach of the General Conditions of Contract (GCC), which entails termination of the 
contract agreement by the SRRDA. 
Further, clause 13.3(a) stipulates that  the Contractor at his cost shall also provide, in 
the joint names of the Employer and the Contractor, insurance cover from the date of 
completion to the end of Defects Liability Period, in the amounts and deductibles stated 
in the Contract Data for personal injury or death, which are due to the Contractor’s risks:
Audit scrutinised 113 sampled works (Roads-55, Bridges-24 and Maintenance-34) 
and found that the contractors did not provide the required insurance cover for work 
execution period as well as for five years (defect liability period) after completion of 
construction for all works. 
In the absence of insurance coverage by the contractors, SRRDA remained at risk of 
bearing financial burden of damages caused to roads /bridges, personal injury/death due 
to accidents during execution. 
Audit noticed that in absence of required insurance cover, SRRDA had to bear an 
expenditure of ₹ 1.32 crore towards restoration of two works in ongoing sites from the 
PMGSY programme fund as detailed below: 
	The work “Construction RCR from Gurung Gaon to Gairi Gaon via Sansaridara” 
was sanctioned for ₹5.99 crore and was awarded to Shri Kailash Rai . The road 
formation and cutting work was completed and protective wall, drainage and 
pavement work was under way. However, heavy rain on the night of 03 July 2019 
caused major landslide, slip and choking drains damaging the protective walls. 
Accordingly, the estimate was revised with additional expenditure on protective 
walls for restoration costing ₹ 95.94 lakh which was met from overall saving of the 
project. 
	The work “Construction RCR from NSH via Upper Gyer” sanctioned for ₹ 6.99 crore 
was awarded (July 2018) to Shri P.D, Denzongpa.  Heavy rain (May 2020) choked 
the drains, slips which ultimately damaged the overall Geometrics of the pavement, 
formation width. Accordingly, the estimate was revised for additional expenditure 
on pavement surface (₹1.62 lakh) and protective wall (₹  34.76 lakh) was provided 
for restoration. The additional financial implication of ₹  36.38 lakh was met from 
overall saving of the project.
Thus, inability on the part of the SRRDA to enforce insurance cover over PMGSY 
works by the contractor led to unwarranted burden of ₹ 1.32 crore on the scheme fund 
which was equivalent to the cost  of construction of one km road.
While accepting the facts, the RDD stated (March 2024) that in accordance to the Para 
9.3.1 of the OM and Clause 13 of GCC, the contractors were directed to provide all risk 
insurance cover, however, it was informed later to RDD that the insurance companies 
were reluctant to provide the insurance cover for PMGSY roads.

balance MA outstanding with the contractor was ₹ 2.48 crore which was not recovered/ 
surrendered by the contractor. Further, bank guarantee had also expired (29 December 
2017) at the time of termination which was not renewed by the contractor. Thus, the 
contractor irregularly retained the advance paid to him for more than four months 
outside government account which resulted in loss of interest amounting to ₹ 6.39 lakh 
to the state exchequer.
Thus, allowing the contractor to retain the MA of ₹ 2.48 crore for more than four months 
even after termination of contract establishes that SRRDA not only could not adhere to 
PMGSY guidelines but also did not exercise financial diligence.
RDD in its reply stated (March 2024) that the matter pertaining to termination of 
contract and re-awarding of the work was intimated to MoRD, GoI and the matter was 
discussed with authorities of GoI and they have suggested that award/ cancellation of 
the work contract is the matter of the State Government. Hence, in view of the fact 
that re-tendering of the work would take substantial amount of time and would cause 
further delay of work and since certain portion of the work had already been completed 
by the contractor so in the best interest of the work and as directed and approved by the 
Government, the same contractor was allowed to resume the work. He has successfully 
completed all the works awarded to him.
The reply is not acceptable as at the time of rescinding the work, RDD should have 
recovered all the dues and the remaining Mobilisation advance from the Contractor. 
SRRDA did not follow due procedure for termination of the contract agreement in first 
place. This shows the lackadaisical approach of SRRDA and undue favour to contractor.

3.3.10.12 Maintenance of assets created under PMGSY
In terms of PMGSY scheme guidelines, a separate maintenance component funded by 
the State Government out of its resources was required to be provided in the DPR. In 
respect of hill roads where construction was done in two stages, interim maintenance, 
clearing of slips, etc. in the period between the first and the second stage were to be done 
departmentally. For maintenance after the second stage, initial five-year maintenance 
was to be contracted out to the same contractor at the time of awarding the work for 
the second stage (Paragraph 8.7 of guidelines). As per Paragraph 32.4 of the Standard 
Bidding Document which forms part of the agreement, contractor shall carry out monthly 
inspection of roads under maintenance, based on which, he shall submit monthly bills on 
e-Marg and e-governance solution for maintenance of rural road under PMGSY  online 
as detailed in subsequent clauses.
The routine maintenance standards shall meet the following minimum requirements: -
(a) Potholes on the road surface to be repaired soon after (but not more than 15 days 
to rectify) ( b) Road shoulders to be maintained in proper condition ( c) Cleaning of 
surface drains, culvert and other cross drainage structures (d) Maintenance of road signs, 
pavement markings etc. ( e) clearing of tree branches to keep the sight distance visible  
(f) maintenance operation required to keep the road traffic worthy at all times during the 
maintenance period.

Paragraph 2.4 of PMGSY Operations Manual stipulated that a State Level Standing

A State Level Standing Committee (SLSC) set up under the chairmanship of the Chief 
Secretary, was responsible for close and effective monitoring of the programme and 
to oversee the timely and proper execution of works . The Committee was to vet the 
Core Network, the CNCPL and CUCPL and clear the annual project proposals. Since

However, no records relating to meetings held and minutes of the SLSC meetings held

SRRDA could not prioritise unconnected eligible habitations while identifying road 
works under PMGSY and expended resources in less priority road works. SRRDA prepare 
estimates by conducting appropriate ground studies and field surveys, which not only 
resulted in infructuous expenditure but also in undue benefit to the contractor. Inability 
of SRRDA in ensuring timely land acquisition resulted in delay in implementation of

3.4 Excess expenditure 
Rural Development Department erroneously paid ₹ 4.32 crore as labour cess was 
included in the estimate for the work and the rate quoted by the contractor was 
inclusive of all taxes including labour cess. Similarly, RDD had also paid ₹ 0.38 
crore (including cess) on inadmissible items, which was avoidable.
According to the Building and Other Construction Workers’ (Regulation of Employment 
and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 (BOCW Act), the Government had implemented 
(September 2010) labour cess at the rate of one per cent on bills on construction works. 
To make Sikkim a Kutchha House free state, the Rural Development Department (RDD) 
identified 6,394 Kutchha house during 2015 and decided to construct 3000 Pucca houses 
under Chief Minister Rural Housing Scheme Phase-I (CMRHM-I) in 2016-17. After 
tendering (December 2016), the RDD awarded (March 2017) the work of construction 
of 3000 houses under CMRHM-Phase-I to the contractor at a total cost of ₹ 379.20 
crore on turnkey basis with stipulated time of completion by March 2019. All the 3,000 
houses were completed by August 2020. 

Chapter III: Economic Sector
115
Subsequently, in December 2018, RDD proposed to construct another 3000 houses 
(which was later increased to 3050 in March 2019) under CMRHM Phase-II later 
renamed Sikkim Garib Abas Yojana (SGAY) at an estimated cost of ₹ 443.49 crore. The 
Department awarded the SGAY works to the same contractor/firm in January 2019 at 
a cost of ₹ 443.49 crore as continuation of phase-I on the same terms and conditions.  
Further, the provision for Television and furniture was also added for all 3050 houses  
(March 2020) at a cost of ₹ 45.05 crore. This work was completed in June 2022. 
Scrutiny of records revealed that Clause 17 of standard conditions of contract entered 
into (February 2019) between RDD and the contractor for construction of the houses 
under SGAY (CMRHM) stipulated that “the rate quoted by the contractor shall be 
deemed to be inclusive of all taxes including labour cess that the contractor will have 
to pay” as labour cess was already included in the estimate for the work. However, in 
contravention of the terms of agreement RDD had paid the contractor as below:
	Per unit house cost - Initially, the work order was issued for construction of 3000 
houses which was later enhanced to 3050 houses (March 2019) at a cost of ₹ 
13,12,478/unit84. 
	Payment of labour cess on civil work - As per estimates, the labour cess was 
included in per unit cost. Accordingly RDD had paid ₹ 4.32 crore to the contractor 
as labour cess component.
Avoidable payment of cess on inadmissible items - As per given codal provision one 
per cent labour cess should have been collected on only construction works, however, it 
was seen that RDD had paid ₹ 0.38 crore (including cess) to the contractor, for purchase 
of TV and furniture to the newly constructed houses under SGAY , which was not 
admissible and led to excess and avoidable expenditure of ₹ 0.38 crore. 
Thus, RDD made irregular payment amounting to ₹ 4.70 crore, comprising cess at one 
per cent of (i) the civil work and (ii) purchase of TV and furniture, which resulted in 
excess expenditure to the tune of ₹ 4.70 crore. 
In reply (November 2023), the Department admitted that the quoted rate of the contractor 
was taking into consideration the labour cess provided in the estimate.
The Department should take urgent action to recover ₹4.70 crore from the contractor. 
The State Government needs to fix responsibility on the officials concerned for such a 
lapse.

4.1.5 Accountability framework
The Companies Act, 2013 and the erstwhile Companies Act, 1956 had not been extended 
to the State of Sikkim. Out of 13 Government Companies existing in the State of Sikkim, 
only four companies were registered under the Companies Act, 1956/2013 while the 
remaining 9 were registered under the ‘Registration of Companies Act, Sikkim, 1961.
The four companies registered and governed by the Companies Act, 2013/1956 included 
Sikkim Urja Limited (SUL), Sikkim Power Transmission Limited (SPTL), Namchi 
Smart City Limited (NSCL) and Gangtok Smart City Development Limited (GSDCL).
During the year 2015-16, one State Government Company 94 acquired 51 per cent of 
equity share capital of SUL, which is the Holding company of SPTL. The other two 
companies (NSCL and GSCDL) were incorporated during 2016-17 and 2017-18 by the 
State Government under the Companies Act, 2013 with headquarters in Darjeeling, West 
Bengal. Thus, all these four companies (SUL, SPTL, NSCL and GSCDL) are covered 
under the definition of a State Government company owned and controlled (directly and 
indirectly) by the State Government.
4.1.5.1 Statutory Audit/Supplementary Audit
The accounts of nine State Government Companies registered under the ‘Registration of 
Companies Act, Sikkim, 1961’ are audited by Statutory Auditors (Chartered Accountants) 
directly appointed by the Board of Directors (BoDs) of the respective Companies. In 
addition to the statutory audit conducted by the Statutory Auditors, supplementary 
audit of these Companies is conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India 
(C&AG) on request of the Governor of the State under Section 20(1) of the Comptroller 
and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.
The accounts of four Companies registered under Companies Act, 2013/1956 are audited 
by the Statutory Auditors (Chartered Accountants) who are appointed by the C&AG. 
In addition to the statutory audit conducted by the Statutory Auditors, supplementary 
audit of these Companies is conducted by the C&AG under Section 143(6) (a) of the

4.1.8.3 Return on Capital Employed
Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) is a profitability metric that measures the long-
term profitability and efficiency of the total capital employed by a company. Companies 
create value when they generate returns on the capital employed. ROCE is an important 
decision metric for long term lenders. ROCE is calculated by dividing a company’s 
earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) by the capital employed104. 
During 2022-23 the overall Capital Employed in 17 working SPSEs as per their latest 
accounts was ₹15,630.61 crore while the ROCE of the SPSEs was 15.42 per cent. Further, 
out of 17 working SPSEs, only 12 SPSEs had positive ROCE while the ROCE of remaining 
five SPSEs105 was not workable due to the negative Capital Employed (Appendix 4.1).
4.1.9 Return on Investment on the basis of Present Value of Investment
The Rate of Real Return (RoRR) measures the profitability and efficiency with which 
equity and similar non-interest bearing capital have been employed, after adjusting them 
for their time value. To determine the RoRR on Government Investments in the State 
PSEs, the investment of State Government in the form of equity, interest free loans 
and grants / subsidies given by the State Government for operational and management 
expenses less the disinvestments has been considered and indexed to their present value 
and summated. The RoRR is then calculated by dividing the Profit After Tax (PAT) of 
the PSEs by the sum of the PV of the Government investments.

State Bank of Sikkim (2021-22)
Comment on Auditors’ Report
1. Refer the positive assurance/opinion expressed by the Auditors on the true and 
correctness of the Accounts of the Bank for the year ended 31 March 2022 vide their 
Audit Report dated 20 July 2022 (refer para 14) and the ‘Disclaimer of Opinion’ 
given on adequacy of provisions maintained by the Bank against bad debts ( refer 
para (iii) - Others under Para 6-Basis for Disclaimer of Audit Opinion). 
As per the criteria prescribed under the ‘Loan Recovery Policy 2014’ (Policy) of the 
Bank, the Bank is required to classify its assets (‘Loans’ and ‘Advances’) into ‘standard 
assets’ and ‘sub-standard assets/non-performing assets (NPAs)’. The ‘Guidelines on 
Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances’ 
(Guidelines) issued by the Bank further prescribed the norms to maintain necessary 
provisions against NPAs, which ranged between 15 per cent (sub-standard assets) and 
100 per cent (loss assets). 
However, the Bank has neither classified its assets in the above categories nor maintained 
the mandatory provisions against NPAs as per the requirements of its own Policy/
Guidelines. Based on the information provided by the Bank, as against Bank’s total loan 
assets of ₹ 2,801.23 crore, the total NPAs (including bad debts and interest suspense) 
worked out to ₹ 1368.79 crore (48.86 per cent) as on 31 March 2022.
Even after considering the minimum mandatory provision of 15 per cent applicable to 
‘sub-standard assets’ (loan assets/accounts which remained NPA for less than or equal 
to 12 months), the Bank was required to maintain provisions of ₹ 205.32 crore against 
the NPAs (₹ 1,368.79 crore) as on 31 March 2022. On the contrary, however, the Bank 
has kept adhoc provisions of ₹ 22.03 crore (cumulative) towards NPAs as on 31 March 
2022. Thus, short provisioning against NPAs has resulted in understatement of ‘Other 
Liabilities & Provisions’ by ₹ 183.29 crore. 
Further, as an impact of the above comment, the ‘Profit for the year’  (₹ 37.04 crore) 
as reported in the financial statements of the Bank for the year ended 31 March 2022 
would turn into ‘Loss’ of ₹ 146.25 crore. As such, the positive assurance/opinion 
expressed by the Auditors on the ‘true and correctness’ of the Accounts of the Bank 
for the year ended 31 March 2022 vide their Audit Report dated 20 July 2022 (refer 
para 14), was not sustainable.

5.12.1 Introduction
Introduction of Goods and Services Tax (GST) has replaced multiple taxes levied and 
collected by the Centre and States. GST, which came into effect from 01 July 2017, is a 
destination-based consumption tax on the supply of goods or services or both levied on 
every value addition. The Centre and States simultaneously levy GST on a common tax 
base. Central GST (CGST) and State GST/Union Territory GST (UTGST) are levied on 
intra-state supplies and Integrated GST (IGST) is levied on inter-state supplies.
Section 59 of the Sikkim Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (SGST Act) stipulates GST 
as a self-assessment based tax, whereby the responsibility for calculating tax liability, 
discharging the computed tax liability and filing returns is vested with the taxpayer. The 
GST returns must be filed online regularly on the common GST portal, failing which 
penalties will be payable. Even if the business has had no tax liability during a particular 
tax period, it must file a nil return mandatorily. Further, Section 61 of the SGST Act read 
with Rule 99 of Sikkim Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 (SGST Rules) stipulate 
that the proper officer may scrutinise the return and related particulars furnished by 
taxpayers, communicate discrepancies to the taxpayers and seek an explanation.
This Subject Specific Compliance Audit (SSCA) was taken up considering the 
significance of the control mechanism envisaged for tax compliance and the oversight 
mechanism of the Commercial Taxes Division, Finance Department, Government of 
Sikkim, (CTD) in this new tax regime.
5.12.2 Audit objectives
This audit was oriented towards providing assurance on adequacy and effectiveness of 
systems and procedures adopted by the CTD with respect to tax compliance under GST 
regime. This audit was taken up with the following audit objectives to seek an assurance 
on:
(i) Whether the rules and procedures were designed to secure an effective check on tax 
compliance and were being duly observed by taxpayers; and
(ii) Whether the scrutiny procedures, internal audit and other compliance functions of 
the Sectors were adequate and effective.
5.12.3 Audit methodology and scope
This SSCA was predominantly conducted based on data analysis, which highlighted 
risk areas and red flags pertaining to the period July 2017 to March 2018. Through data 
analysis, a set of 12 deviations were identified across the domains of input tax credit, 
discharge of tax liability, registration and return filing. Such deviations were followed 
up through a centralised audit 120, whereby these deviations were communicated to 
the relevant Sectors and action taken by the Sectors on the identified deviations was 
ascertained without involving field visits. The centralised audit was supplemented by a

related ledger accounts, invoices, agreements etc.

The returns and related attachments and information were accessed through the State 
CTD’s tax application (http://www.sikkimtax.gov.in/) as much as feasible to examine 
data/documents relating to taxpayers (viz. returns, tax payment, etc.). The detailed audit 
also involved accessing relevant granular records from the taxpayers such as invoices 
through the Sectors. This apart, compliance functions of the Sectors such as scrutiny of 
returns, conduct of internal audit, action on late filers/non-filers etc. were also reviewed 
in selected Sectors.
In Sikkim, the functional organisation of the CTD under GST is based on Sectors or 
nature of business (such as Manufacturer, Trader, Service Provider, etc.). Therefore, the 
audit of functions of selected Sectors was taken up. 
The review of the scrutiny of returns by the CTD and verification of taxpayers’ records 
covered the period from July 2017 to March 2018, while the audit of the functions of 
selected Sectors covered the period from July 2017 to March 2021. The SSCA covered 
only State administered taxpayers. The field audit was conducted from 1 April 2022 to 
1 February 2023.
Entry Conference of this SSCA was held on 1 April 2022 with a team of officers from the 
CTD headed by the Commissioner in which the audit objectives, sample selection, audit 
scope and methodology were discussed. The Exit Conference was held on 01  February 
2023 with a team of concerned officers from the CTD in which the audit findings were 
discussed. The views expressed by the CTD team during the Exit Conference and 
the written replies to the draft report have been suitably incorporated in the relevant 
paragraphs.
5.12.4 Audit sample 
A data-driven approach was adopted for planning, as also to determine the nature and 
extent of substantive audit. The sample for this SSCA comprised a set of deviations 
identified through data analysis for centralised audit that did not involve field visits; a 
sample of taxpayers for detailed audit that involved field visits and scrutiny of taxpayer’s 
records at the CTD’s premises; and a sample of Sectors for evaluating the compliance 
functions of the Sectors.
There were three distinct parts of this SSCA as under:
(i) Part I-Audit of Sectors: Three Sectors with jurisdiction over more than one 
selected sample of cases for detailed audit were considered as the sample of Sectors 
for evaluation of their oversight functions. 
(ii) Part II-Centralised Audit: The sample for centralised audit was selected by 
identification of high-value or high-risk deviations from rules and inconsistencies 
between returns through data analysis for evaluation of the adequacy and 
effectiveness of the scrutiny procedure of the CTD. Accordingly, 93 cases were 
selected for centralised audit under this SSCA.
(iii) Part III-Detailed Audit: It was conducted by accessing taxpayers’ records through 
Sectors for evaluation of the extent of tax compliance by taxpayers. The sample of 
taxpayers for detailed audit was selected on the basis of various risk parameters such 
as excess ITC, tax liability mismatch, disproportionate exempted turnover to total 
turnover and irregular ITC reversal. Fourteen taxpayers selected for detailed audit

b) Lack of action on late-filers and non-filers
Section 46 of the SGST Act read with Rule 68 of SGST Rules stipulates issue of a 
notice in Form GSTR-3A requiring filing of return within fifteen days if the taxpayer 
had failed to file the return within the due date. Further, Section 62 of SGST Act read 
with Rule 100 of SGST Rule stipulates that in case, the taxpayer fails to file the returns 
even after such notice, the competent officers may proceed to assess the tax liability of 
the said person to the best of their judgement, considering all the relevant material which 
is available or gathered and issue an assessment order in Form ASMT-13. Section 29(2)
(c) of the SGST Act provides that the proper officer may cancel the registration of a 
person from such date, including any retrospective date, as he may deem fit, where, any 
registered person, other than a person specified in clause (b), has not furnished returns 
for a continuous period of six months.
Filing of returns is related to payment of tax as the due date for both the actions are 
same. This implies risk of non-payment of tax/penalty in the case of non-filers.
To assess the CTD’s action on late/non-filers of the returns, information 127 on non/late 
filers identified and action taken by three selected Sectors during July 2017 to March 
2021 were called for in Audit. Despite issue of several reminders, no information was 
furnished to the Audit till date (November 2023). In this regard, however, the CTD 
responded on 12 September 2022 that non-filers are not applicable under GST regime. 
The contention of the CTD is not acceptable as Section 29(2) (c) of the SGST Act clearly 
provides that the proper officer may cancel the registration of a person from such date, 
including any retrospective date, as he may deem fit, where any registered person, other 
than a person specified in clause (b), has not furnished returns for a continuous period 
of six months.

c)    Inadequacy of verification mechanism for cancellation of registration
Section 29(1) of SGST Act, 2017 stipulates that the proper officer may, either on his own 
motion, or on application filed by registered person or his legal heir cancel the registration 
having regard to circumstances where the business has been discontinued, change in 
constitution of business or the taxable person is no longer liable to be registered. 
Section 29(2) of the SGST Act, 2017 allows for suo moto cancellation of the registration 
of taxpayer by tax officer on the grounds of contravention of the Acts or Rules by the 
taxpayer, composition  taxpayers not filing return for three consecutive tax periods, 
normal taxpayers not filing return for continuous period of six months, registered persons 
not commencing business within six months from date of registration and registration 
obtained by means of fraud, willful misstatement or suppression of facts.
Rule 22(1) of SGST Rules, 2017 prescribes that where proper officer has reasons to 
believe that registration of a person is liable to be cancelled under Section 29, he shall 
issue a notice to such person in form GST REG-17, requiring him to show cause, within 
a period of seven working days, from the date of serving of such notice, as to why his 
registration should not be cancelled. 
To assess CTD’s action on cancellation of registration, information 132 pertaining to 
action taken for cancellation of registration by the selected Sectors during July 2017 to 
March 2021 was called for in Audit.

State till date (November 2023). Therefore, in the absence of complete information 
on cancellation of registrations initiated by tax authorities and follow up action taken 
by them, the function of the Sectors on verification mechanism for cancellation of 
registration could not be assessed.

(i) ITC mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A
GSTR-2A is a purchase related dynamic tax return that is automatically generated 
for each business by the GST portal, whereas GSTR-3B is a monthly return in which 
summary of outward supplies along with ITC declared and payment of tax are self-
declared by the taxpayer. 
To analyse the veracity of ITC utilisation, relevant data were extracted from GSTR-
3B and GSTR-2A for the year 2017-18, and the ITC paid as per suppliers’ details was 
matched with the ITC credit availed by the taxpayer. 
Audit observed that in case of a taxpayer, M/s Intas Pharmaceuticals  (GSTIN - 
11AAACI5120L1Z1) under Industries Sector, ITC available as per GSTR-2A was ₹ 28.74 
crore and the ITC availed in table 4(A)(5) of GSTR-3B was ₹ 30.15 crore (including 
ITC ₹ 2.23 crore availed in the subsequent year 2018-19 from Table 8C of GSTR-9). 
This resulted in mismatch of ITC availed for ₹ 1.41 crore which was communicated to 
the CTD on 19 May 2022. In response, CTD furnished (April 2023) three justifications

for the excess ITC as follows:
(a) Total ITC for ₹ 29.82 crore and not ₹ 28.75 crore was being arrived after deducting 
import from SEZ. This conte ntion was not acceptable as the ITC availed figure 
arrived at by Audit did not include the figures of table 4(A) (1) of GSTR-3B 
(imports). 
(b) The excess ITC was further justified by furnishing the amended invoices pertaining 
to ITC of ₹ 0.97 crore. However, the original invoices in this case were not produced 
to Audit. Therefore, the Audit was unable to verify the claim of amendment of 
invoices in this case.
(c) There was ITC of ₹ 0.04 crore pertaining to purchase invoices of 2017-18 uploaded 
by the suppliers in 2018-19, this was checked in GSTR-1 of suppliers for 2018-19 
and found correct. Therefore, the observation is amended by Audit to that extent. 
Hence, excess ITC of ₹ 1.37 crore was due to the state exchequer from M/s Intas 
Pharmaceuticals.
(ii) ITC availed under RCM without payment of tax in GSTR-3B/ GSTR-9
Under the Reverse Charge Mechanism, the liability to pay tax is fixed on the recipient 
of supply of goods or services instead of the supplier or provider in respect of certain 
categories of goods or services or both under Section 9(3) or Section 9(4) of the SGST 
Act, 2017 and under sub-section (3) or sub-section (4) of Section 5 of the SGST Act, 2017.
GSTR-9 is an annual return to be filed once for each financial year, by the registered 
taxpayers who were regular taxpayers, including SEZ units and SEZ developers. The 
taxpayers are required to furnish details of purchases, sales, input tax credit or refund 
claimed, or demand created etc.
To analyse the veracity of ITC availed on tax paid under Reverse Charge Mechanism 
(RCM) for the year 2017-18, the datasets pertaining to GSTR-3B and annual return 
GSTR-9 were compared to check whether the ITC availed on RCM was restricted to the 
extent of tax paid. 
Audit observed that in case of a taxpayer, M/s ATC Telecom Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. 
(GSTIN - 11AACCT1282E1ZW) under Service Sector, ITC available in table 3.1(d) 
of GSTR-3B was ₹ 0.03 crore and the ITC availed in table 4A (2) & (3) of GSTR-
3B was ₹ 0.31 crore resulting in mismatch of ITC availed for ₹ 0.28 crore. This was 
communicated to the CTD on 19 May 2022 followed by reminders on 19 July 2022 and 
31 August 2022. No response was received from the CTD (November 2023).

(xii) Short/Non-payment of interest
Section 50 of the SGST Act stipulates that every person liable to pay tax in accordance 
with the provisions of this Act or the Rules made there under but fails to pay the tax or 
any part thereof to the Government within the period prescribed, shall for the period for 
which the tax or any part thereof remains unpaid, pay interest at the rate notified.
The extent of short/non-payment of interest on account of delayed remittance of tax 
during 2017-18 was identified using the tax paid details in GSTR-3B and the date of 
filing of the GSTR-3B. Only the net tax liability (cash component) had been considered 
to work out the interest payable.

issue was communicated to the CTD on 19 May 2022 followed by reminders on 19 July

5.12.6.3  Detailed Audit 
In a self-assessment regime, the onus of compliance with the law is on the taxpayer. The 
role of the CTD is to establish and maintain an efficient tax administration mechanism 
to provide oversight. With a finite level of resources, for an effective tax administration, 
to ensure compliance with law and collection of revenue, an efficient governance 
mechanism is essential. An IT driven compliance model enables maintaining a non-
discretionary regime of governance on scale and facilitates a targeted approach to 
enforce compliance.
From an external audit perspective, Audit also focused on a data-driven risk-based 
approach. Thus, apart from identifying inconsistencies/deviations in GST returns 
through data analysis, a detailed audit of GST returns was also conducted as a part of 
this review. A risk-based sample of 14 taxpayers was selected for this part of the review. 
The methodology adopted was to initially conduct a desk review of GST returns and 
financial statements filed by the taxpayers as part of the GSTR-9C and other records 
available in the back-end system to identify potential risk areas, inconsistencies/
deviations, and red flags. Desk Review was carried out at the office of the Accountant 
General (Audit), Sikkim. Based on desk review results, detailed audit was conducted 
in the office of the Commissioner, CTD, Government of Sikkim, by requisitioning 
corresponding granular records of taxpayers such as purchase invoices, sales invoices, 
and other relevant documents to identify causative factors of the identified risks and to 
evaluate compliance by taxpayers. The details of risks identified are given in Appendix 
5.6 and 5.7.
In reply to audit requisitions for information/documents like annual financial statements 
and purchase/sales invoices required for detailed audit, the Department furnished records 
only in case of one taxpayer out of 14 selected taxpayers.
In seven cases, no information/records were furnished by the CTD as required by the 
Audit. The details are in Appendix 5.8 (a) and the top three cases are listed in Table 5.21.

As brought out in the previous paragraphs, detailed audit involved a desk review of GST 
returns and other basic records to identify risks and red flags, which were followed up 
by field audit to identify the extent of non-compliance by taxpayers and action taken by 
the CTD. Noncompliance by taxpayers at various stages ultimately impacts the veracity 
of returns filed, utilisation of ITC and discharge of tax payments. As such, the audit 
findings are categorised under: (a) Returns (b) Utilisation of ITC (c) Discharge of tax 
liability and (d) Other findings.

(i)  Non-payment of interest taxpayers

return of inward and outward supplies of goods or services or both, input tax credit 
availed, tax payable, tax paid and such other particulars as may be prescribed are required 
to be filed on or before the twentieth day of the month succeeding such calendar month 
or part thereof.

GSTR-1: Section 37 of SGST Act read with Rule 59 of SGST Rules provides for filing

(b)  Audit findings relating to Utilisation of Input Tax Credit 
Input Tax Credit (ITC) means the Goods and Services Tax (GST) paid by a taxable 
person on purchase of goods and/or services that are used in the course or furtherance of 
business. To avoid cascading effect of taxes, credit of taxes paid on input supplies can 
be used to set-off for payment of taxes on outward supplies.

The audit observations pertaining to utilisation of ITC are as follows:
(i)  ITC mismatch between GSTR-2A and GSTR-3B
Section 16(2) of the SGST Act prescribes the conditions for availing ITC. The 
prerequisites for availing ITC are:
•	 Taxpayer should be in possession of tax invoice or any other specified tax paying 
document
•	 Taxpayer has received the goods or services
•	 Tax has actually been paid by the supplier 
•	 Taxpayer has furnished the return to avail the ITC 
•	 The value of the goods or services along with the tax should have been paid to the 
supplier within 180 days from the date of issue of invoice. 
Rule 36 of SGST Rules prescribe the documentary requirements for claiming ITC. A 
taxpayer can avail ITC based on (a) Invoice issued by a supplier of goods or services or 
both, (b) Invoice issued by recipient along with proof of payment of tax, (c) A debit note 
issued by supplier, (d) Bill of entry or similar document prescribed under Customs Act, 
(e) Revised invoice and (f) Document issued by Input Service Distributor. No ITC shall 
be availed beyond September of the following financial year to which invoice pertains 
or date of filing of annual return, whichever is earlier.
To check the correctness of the ITC claim, Audit compared the ITC claimed by the 
taxpayers with the ITC available in GSTR-2A. Out of total 14 sample cases, mismatch 
were observed in 11 cases where taxpayers had availed excess ITC of ₹ 13.90 crore.

Section 9(4) of the SGST Act, 2017 stipulates that the State tax in respect of the supply 
of taxable goods or services or both by a supplier, who is not registered, to a registered

be claimed subject to the payment of tax.

(iii)  Incorrect availment of ISD credit
Section 2(61) of the SGST Act defines “Input Service Distributor” (ISD) as an office of 
the supplier of goods or services or both which receives tax invoices towards the receipt 
of input services and issues a prescribed document for the purposes of distributing 
the ITC to a supplier of taxable goods or services or both having the same Permanent 
Account Number (PAN) as that of the said office. Section 20 of the Act prescribes the 
manner of distribution of credit by ISD. As per Section 20(2), ISD may distribute the 
credit available for distribution in the same month in which it is availed. ISD shall issue 
invoice in accordance with the provisions made under Rule 39(1) of the SGST Rules.
In this regard, Rule 54 (1A)(a) of the SGST Rules provides for a registered person, 
having the same PAN and State code as an ISD, to issue an invoice or, as the case may 
be, a credit or debit note to transfer the credit of common input services to the ISD.
Out of 14 sample taxpayers, Audit observed mismatch in case of one taxpayer i.e. M/s 
Alembic Pharmaceuticals (GSTIN - 11AAICA5591M1ZG) for ₹ 0.17 crore. The taxpayer 
received ITC of ₹ 1.27 crore from ISD through GSTR-6 whereas the taxpayer had declared 
an amount of ₹ 1.44 crore as ITC received from ISD in Table 6G of GSTR9. This indicated 
excess availing of ITC under ISD by ₹ 0.17 crore along with the interest of ₹ 0.17 crore150.
This was intimated to CTD on 14 July 2022 and the reasons for inconsistencies and details 
of action taken, if any, under Section 61 of the SGST Act was also called for. In response, 
the CTD intimated (12 September 2022) that as GSTR-6 of the ISD was not integrated 
with the State GST portal, data would be obtained from the concerned taxpayer and 
manual verification would be conducted. The CTD further added that similar verification 
shall be conducted for other taxpayers who have availed credit from ISDs. The report of 
verification would be forwarded to Audit. It was further replied (6 April 2023) and clarified

Section 17(2) of the SGST Act, 2017 stipulates that where the goods or services or 
both are used by the registered person partly for effecting taxable supplies including 
zero-rated supplies under this Act or under the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act 
and partly for effecting exempt supplies under the said Acts, the amount of credit shall 
be restricted to so much of the input tax as is attributable to the said taxable supplies 
including zero-rated supplies.

respect of inputs or input services, which attract the provisions of sub-section (1) or sub-
section (2) of section 17.
Rule 42 (i) of the SGST Rules 2017 stipulates that ‘the amount of input tax credit 
attributable towards exempt supplies, denoted as D1 and calculated as D1= (E÷F) × 
C2 where, ‘E’ is the aggregate value of exempt supplies during the tax period, ‘F’ is the 
total turnover in the State of the registered person during the tax period and C2 is the 
common credit.

5.12.7 Conclusion
The Subject Specific Compliance Audit on Department’s Oversight on GST Payments 
and Returns Filing was undertaken with an objective of assessing the adequacy of 
the system in monitoring returns filing and tax payments by the taxpayers, extent of 
compliance by the taxpayers and other departmental oversight functions. The audit was 
predominantly based on data analysis, which highlighted risk areas, red flags and in 
some cases, rule-based deviations and logical inconsistencies in GST returns filed for 
2017-18 by the taxpayers.
The department was unable to provide records pertaining to scrutiny of returns, action 
taken on late/non-filers, cancellation of registrations as well as on internal audit. This 
indicated that the oversight functions of Sectors were not done as envisaged by the 
GST Act and Rules. Audit also observed that the CTD had not formulated any Standard 
Operating Procedure (SOP) for scrutiny functions as done by the CBIC. Therefore, 
due to absence of an institutional mechanism in the Sectors to establish and maintain 
effective oversight on returns filing, taxpayers’ compliance and tax payments, cases of 
non-compliance by taxpayers were observed during the Audit. 
Out of total 93 inconsistencies/mismatches identified during Centralised Audit, in 
55 cases Department did not furnish any response to audit queries. Upon analysing the 
responses of the Department received in remaining 38 cases, 22 cases involving amount 
of ₹ 3.71 crore turned out to be compliance deficiencies. A relatively higher rate of 
deficiencies was noticed in mismatch of ITC availed between annual returns and books 
of accounts, excess RCM ITC availed, mismatch in tax paid between books of accounts 
and returns and incorrect availment of ISD credit. In four cases, the CTD recovered the 
amount of ₹ 0.24 crore from the taxpayers on compliance deviations being pointed out 
by the Audit. The data entry errors caused the inconsistencies in four cases and 12 cases 
had valid explanations. 
As regards Detailed Audit, out of samples of 14 taxpayers in seven cases other granular 
records were not produced at all and in six cases partial records were produced, 
which significantly limited the scope for Detailed Audit. Detailed Audit among others 
also pointed towards non-compliance on five major issues with tax implication of

₹ 30.78 crore: (i) Non-payment of interest by nine taxpayers of ₹ 1.05 crore (ii) mismatch 
of tax liability of ₹ 0.57 crore involving eight taxpayers, (iii) mismatch between returns 
in availing ITC of ₹ 13.90 crore by 11 taxpayers, (iv) unreconciled ITC of ₹ 15.11 crore 
involving four taxpayers (v) unreconciled taxes paid of ₹ 0.16 crore by two taxpayers. In 
five cases, tax amount of ₹ 0.19 crore was paid by the taxpayers at the instance of Audit.
5.12.8 Summary of Recommendations
After evaluation of records furnished and analysis of data available in the State system, 
the following recommendations are made:
1. The CTD may put in place proper mechanism for scrutiny of returns to ensure 
compliance of rules pertaining to returns filing and tax payments by all taxpayers. 
The CTD may prepare a Standard Operating Procedure for manual scrutiny of 
returns in line with one prepared by CBIC, for use till automation of scrutiny is 
completed.
2. CTD may establish mechanism to regularly identify late-filers and non-filers and 
take necessary steps to recover tax, interest and late fee from them.
3. CTD may establish mechanism to regularly identify taxpayers who have not filed 
GST returns for more than six months and take necessary steps to recover applicable 
tax, interest and late fee from them and cancel the registrations.
4. CTD may urgently pursue the 55 inconsistencies/deviations pointed out by Audit 
for which responses have not been provided and intimate the results there-of.
5. The CTD may conduct similar data analysis (as conducted by Audit for Centralised/ 
limited Audit) of GST returns and other related data of all the taxpayers under State 
jurisdiction to identify inconsistencies and take necessary steps to recover dues 
from the taxpayers wherever applicable. 
6. The department may initiate remedial action for all the compliance deviations 
pointed out through this report before they get time-barred.

6.2 Planning and conduct of audit
Audit process starts with the assessment of risks faced by various departments of the 
Government based on expenditure incurred, criticality/complexity of activities, level of 
delegated financial powers, assessment of overall internal controls, etc.
After completion of audit of each unit on a test-check basis, Inspection Reports (IRs) 
containing audit observations are issued to the heads of the departments.  The departments 
are required to furnish replies to the audit findings within one month of receipt of the IRs.  
Whenever replies are received, audit findings are either settled based on reply/action 
taken or the audited entities are required to take further action for compliance.  Some of 
the important audit observations arising out of these IRs are processed for inclusion in 
the Audit Reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.  These Audit Reports 
are submitted to the Governor of the State under Article 151 of the Constitution of India 
for laying on the table of the Legislature for taking further appropriate action.

this Central Sector Scheme in January 2015. The objective of the scheme was to develop 
tourist circuits and promote the cultural and heritage value of the country. Further, the

6.3.8					Identification	and	Selection	of	circuits
6.3.8.1   Improper selection of Circuits/ Destinations
Identification of the tourist circuit and the destinations is a vital component of the 
scheme. The tourist circuits/destinations were to be identified by MoT in consultation 
with the stakeholders and States based on a pre-dominant tourism theme, considering 
factors such as current tourist traffic, connectivity potential and significance attached to 
the sites, holistic tourist experience etc. 
However, audit observed that the DPR prepared by the department did not have any 
reference to such consultations, indicating absence of the same. Neither was the basis for 
selection of projects/components specified in the Cabinet Memos nor did the Department 
conduct any feasibility study before implementing the scheme.
Such deficiencies in planning affected the overall execution and implementation of the 
projects as audit noticed numerous cases of delay in completion of the projects, non-
utilisation of infrastructure, improper utilisation of infrastructure created as elucidated 
in succeeding paragraphs.
In reply, the Department stated (March 2024) that meetings were held at different 
occasions with both internally as well as with various stakeholders to discuss and 
identify the requirements of tourism facilities along with tourist circuit to be undertaken 
under SD schemes however, minutes of these meeting could not be traced. The reply of 
the department was not acceptable as department  had neither produced any document 
in support of holding of meetings with stakeholders nor was any reference made in the 
DPR regarding consultation with various stakeholders.
6.3.8.2   Deficiencies in preparation of DPR  
As per the scheme guidelines, a comprehensive DPR should be prepared for each circuit 
after consultation with the respective State Government/UT Administration, Local 
Bodies, other stake holders for the components to be funded by public funding. The 
DPR shall be prepared as per toolkit of Ministry of Tourism. A toolkit was prepared 
by Ministry of Tourism to help State Governments/Department of Tourism/Tourism 
Development Corporation in preparation of Detailed Project Reports to be submitted 
for funding under Swadesh Darshan Scheme to Ministry of Tourism, Government of 
India. Further, according to Para 4(a) of Part B of toolkit, Destination wise Assessment 
of Tourist profiling consisting of Category of tourists, Footfall of tourists, Carrying 
capacity of the destination/site, duration of stay, etc., have to be included in the DPR. 
However, audit noticed that instead of destination-wise information, State-wide 
information was provided in the DPRs. Further, information regarding profiling of tourista 
and socio-economic benefits required to be included in the DPR were not included. 
In the absence of such vital data, performance in respect of important objectives of 
the scheme such as increase in tourist traffic in the identified circuits and employment 
generation could not be evaluated or assessed.
In reply the department accepted (March 2024) that destination-wise data was not 
provided and overall state data were taken in the DPR.

According to para 4.6 of the revised scheme guidelines 2017, if there is any escalation/
variation from approved DPR, SGs/UT Administrations must inform MoT and seek its 
approval for the same before commencing work on the component. Further, Para 7 of 
sanction letter (30 June 2015) of MoT Government of India stipulated that funds will be

However, deviations from DPR with respect to cost, changes in scope of work and 
execution of works not included in DPR were noticed in nine cases. The details of the

The above deviations were done without the approval of the GoI in violation of the

In reply, Department accepted (March 2024) that certain revision of items for befitting 
the requirements as per site condition and necessity were undertaken in the best interest 
of the project. 
Reply was not acceptable as the Department had neither nor informed MoT nor taken 
approval from MoT before commencing the deviation, in contrast to the guidelines. 
Further, requirement and site conditions were to be brought to the notice of MoT before 
implementing the deviations.

6.3.9.1 Infrastructures created in Monastery and Temple land
According to Para 8.3 of Scheme guidelines issued (2015) and para 4.3 of revised 
guidelines 2017, improvement/investment in assets/structures owned by the private 
entities were not admissible under the schemes. In this connection, TCAD submitted 
the land availability certificate along with the DPR to MoT stating that all lands were 
free from encumbrance to accommodate all the features of the project under Swadesh 
Darshan and the lands were in possession of the Department.
Scrutiny of records revealed that tourist infrastructure in nine destinations were 
constructed in the land belonging to either Monastery or temple as detailed in Appendix 
6.4, which resulted in affecting the State’s ownership of the project/assets as well as its 
access to revenue from the project.
In reply, Department stated (March 2024) that the temples and monasteries serve as 
significant tourist attractions and vital sources of livelihood within the state. Monastic 
tourism plays a central role in promoting tourism. It’s essential to involve these religious 
sites in tourism circuits to enrich the overall experience. The reply of the department 
was not tenable, since creation of infrastructure in private land was not admissible as 
per the scheme guidelines.

6.3.11    Monitoring and impact assessment
6.3.11.1 Formation of State Level Monitoring Committee
As per revised guidelines of the scheme, the States UT Administration shall appoint 
a State Level Monitoring Committee for timely implementation of the project. The 
purpose of the committee is to provide feedback on the progress of implementation to the 
GoI regularly. On the basis of this, the Department constituted a monitoring committee 
consisting of six members headed by Chief Engineer as Chairman on 10.02.2016 after a 
lapse of seven months of issue of sanctioned letter.  
Scrutiny of records revealed that no records existed in the department to indicate that 
SLMC met regularly after its formation. This is particularly important since audit has 
observed numerous cases of delays in implementation of the projects as indicated in 
paragraph 6.3.9.3. Since monitoring of the overall progress of the scheme was one 
of the objectives of formation of SLMC, the monitoring mechanism envisaged by the 
scheme guidelines was rendered ineffective as no meetings were held by the SLMC. In 
absence of effective functioning of the monitoring mechanism, delay in completion of 
works ranging from four months to 37 months could not be avoided. 
In reply, Department stated (March 2024) that State Level Monitoring Committee 
headed by the Chief Engineer has been constantly monitoring the Schemes right from 
conceptualisation till completion, but proceedings of the meetings have not been 
recorded. Reply was not tenable in the absence of proceeding of the meetings.

(QPR) of the project 
As per the standard procedures for processing projects sanctioned before October 2017 
under Swadesh Darshan Scheme, all the States shall mandatorily submit MPRs in the 
prescribed formats giving physical and financial progress to the ministry so that ministry 
can review the progress of the projects.

Tourism, Government of Sikkim, it was seen in the MPR that the components approved

As per paragraph 15 of scheme guidelines, the outcome of the Integrated Development 
of the tourist circuit in mission mode would be measured in terms of increase in tourist 
traffic, employment generation, and increase in revenue generation, etc. in the identified

7.3 Performance Audit on Solid Waste Management in Urban Local Bodies
Government of Sikkim (GoS), in the State Policy on Solid Waste Management Strategy 
notified in April 2019 has envisioned to establish a ‘Zero Waste System’ for Solid Waste 
Management in the state by the year 2030 with a mission to enable the community to 
visualise experience and own up utilisation of resources along with conservation of 
environment for sustainable development.
The performance audit of Solid Waste Management (SWM) in Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs) for the period 2018-23 was carried out (August- September 2022 and May-June 
2023) with the objective to assess the efficacy of SWM including collection, segregation, 
storage, transportation and disposal of waste. The ULBs stated to have collected entire 
quantity of solid waste generated (68.9 tonnes per day (tpd) during 2022-23, of which 
23.78 tpd was processed and remaining 45.12 tpd was dumped at landfill/ dumpsite. While 
the State Government formulated (April 2019) ‘State Policy on Solid Waste Management 
Strategy and Action plan for SWM’, by laws, etc. and successfully implemented green 
protocol for waste reduction through ban on use of plastic, polystyrene, ethens, etc,; 
the ULBs had neither prepared SWM Plan nor complied with the action plan circulated 
by the State Government in respect of Cluster Plan for Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) 
management, disposal of waste at cluster level, stringent law for source segregation and 
resource recovery. While the segregation of waste was not in practice by majority of 
the households, transportation of waste was done by the ULBs in uncovered vehicles 
without any partition thereby mixing various types of waste. Processing of waste was

7.3.3 Audit objectives 
The objectives of the Performance audit were to assess whether:
	Strategy and planning of SWM in ULBs was commensurate with the solid waste 
generated and concurrent with the prevailing legal framework;
	Financial management for discharging SWM functions were efficient and effective;

transportation, disposal and social inclusion of informal waste workers were 
effective, efficient and economical; and
